title: Who’s who
text: Each entry says in a sentence or two what the body does and links to the laws in this wiki that create it, give it authority, or set how it is overseen. Acronyms are the ones used on the Hill. Every entry links to the body’s official site or to the section of the U.S. Code that establishes it.

title: Who’s who
text:
Congress: committees 9

House Committee on Armed Services (HASC)
Authorizes the Defense Department and the national security programs of the Energy Department and writes the House version of the annual NDAA. Its jurisdiction follows Title 10: forces, personnel, acquisition, and Defense Department security cooperation.
Laws in this wiki: NDAA (annual), Title 10 U.S.C., Goldwater-Nichols Act, Security Cooperation (Ch. 16), Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative.
Official source: House Armed Services Committee


Senate Committee on Armed Services (SASC)
The Senate counterpart to HASC: writes the Senate NDAA and also confirms senior Defense Department civilians and military officers, which gives it a second lever over defense policy.
Laws in this wiki: NDAA (annual), Title 10 U.S.C., Goldwater-Nichols Act, Security Cooperation (Ch. 16), Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative.
Official source: Senate Armed Services Committee


House Committee on Foreign Affairs (HFAC)
Jurisdiction in the House over the State Department, foreign assistance, arms sales, export controls, most sanctions, and war powers and use-of-force resolutions. Receives arms sale notifications under the Arms Export Control Act.
Laws in this wiki: Foreign Assistance Act, Arms Export Control Act, War Powers Resolution, IEEPA, Export Control Reform Act, Foreign Military Financing, IMET, Foreign Military Sales.
Official source: House Foreign Affairs Committee


Senate Committee on Foreign Relations (SFRC)
Jurisdiction in the Senate over the State Department, treaties, foreign assistance, arms sales, and authorizations for the use of force. Also handles ambassadorial and State Department nominations and advice and consent to treaties.
Laws in this wiki: Foreign Assistance Act, Arms Export Control Act, War Powers Resolution, Case-Zablocki Act, Foreign Military Financing, IMET, Foreign Military Sales.
Official source: Senate Foreign Relations Committee


House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence (HPSCI)
Created by House rule in 1977 to oversee the intelligence community. Writes the annual intelligence authorization and receives covert action findings and notifications of significant intelligence activities.
Laws in this wiki: National Security Act, Intel Oversight Act, IRTPA, FISA.
Official source: House Permanent Select Committee on Intelligence


Senate Select Committee on Intelligence (SSCI)
Created by Senate resolution in 1976, after the Church Committee’s investigation, to oversee the intelligence community. Writes the Senate intelligence authorization and considers nominations for senior intelligence posts.
Laws in this wiki: National Security Act, Intel Oversight Act, IRTPA, FISA.
Official source: Senate Select Committee on Intelligence


House Committee on Appropriations (House Appropriations)
Its Defense subcommittee writes the annual Defense appropriations act, and its subcommittee on National Security, Department of State, and Related Programs writes the State-foreign operations act. Approves reprogramming and transfer requests informally through the committee notification process.
Laws in this wiki: Defense appropriations (annual), State-foreign ops appropriations, Sec. 8005 transfers, Coup restriction (Sec. 7008).
Official source: House Appropriations Committee


Senate Committee on Appropriations (Senate Appropriations)
The Senate counterpart: its Defense subcommittee and its subcommittee on State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs write the Senate versions of the two annual acts.
Laws in this wiki: Defense appropriations (annual), State-foreign ops appropriations, Sec. 8005 transfers, Coup restriction (Sec. 7008).
Official source: Senate Appropriations Committee


Senate Committee on Banking, Housing, and Urban Affairs (Senate Banking)
In the Senate, sanctions under IEEPA, export controls, the Defense Production Act, and foreign investment review go to Banking rather than Foreign Relations, which makes it a central sanctions committee.
Laws in this wiki: IEEPA, Export Control Reform Act, Defense Production Act, FIRRMA (CFIUS), CAATSA.
Official source: Senate Banking Committee

title: Who’s who
text:
Congress: support agencies 2

Government Accountability Office (GAO)
Congress’s audit and investigative agency, headed by the Comptroller General. Issues decisions on appropriations law, reports impoundments the President has not, and may sue to release withheld funds.
Laws in this wiki: Impoundment Control Act, Antideficiency Act.
Official source: GovInfo, 31 U.S.C. 702


Congressional Research Service (CRS)
The nonpartisan research agency in the Library of Congress that works only for members, committees, and their staff. Its public reports are a standard starting point on nearly every law in this wiki.
Laws in this wiki: none; it rests on other law or on regulation.
Official source: GovInfo, 2 U.S.C. 166

title: Who’s who
text:
Executive branch 16

National Security Council (NSC)
Created by the National Security Act of 1947 to advise the President on integrating domestic, foreign, and military policy. Its staff, led by the national security adviser, runs the interagency policy process.
Laws in this wiki: National Security Act.
Official source: GovInfo, 50 U.S.C. 3021


Office of Management and Budget (OMB)
Prepares the President’s budget and apportions appropriated funds to agencies, which makes it the point where impoundment disputes usually begin. Approves Defense Department general transfers.
Laws in this wiki: Antideficiency Act, Impoundment Control Act, Sec. 8005 transfers.
Official source: GovInfo, 31 U.S.C. 501


Department of Defense (DoD)
The executive department, created in 1949 from the National Military Establishment, under a civilian Secretary of Defense with authority, direction, and control over the military departments and combatant commands.
Laws in this wiki: National Security Act, NSA Amendments (1949), DoD Reorganization Act (1958), Goldwater-Nichols Act, NDAA (annual), Defense appropriations (annual).
Official source: GovInfo, 10 U.S.C. 111


Joint Chiefs of Staff (JCS)
The senior uniformed leaders of the services. The Chairman is the principal military adviser to the President and Secretary of Defense; since Goldwater-Nichols the Joint Chiefs are outside the operational chain of command.
Laws in this wiki: National Security Act, Goldwater-Nichols Act.
Official source: GovInfo, 10 U.S.C. 151


Combatant commands
The geographic and functional commands, such as Central Command and Cyber Command, that conduct military operations. The chain of command runs from the President through the Secretary of Defense to the combatant commanders.
Laws in this wiki: Goldwater-Nichols Act, DoD Reorganization Act (1958), Section 394 (cyber).
Official source: GovInfo, 10 U.S.C. 161


U.S. Special Operations Command (SOCOM)
The unified command for special operations forces, created by the Nunn-Cohen Amendment with its own budget authority. Conducts programs such as those under Section 127e.
Laws in this wiki: Nunn-Cohen Amendment, Section 127e.
Official source: GovInfo, 10 U.S.C. 167


Defense Security Cooperation Agency (DSCA)
The Defense Department agency that administers Foreign Military Sales, Foreign Military Financing, IMET, excess defense articles, and most Title 10 security cooperation programs. Sends major arms sale notifications to Congress.
Laws in this wiki: Foreign Military Sales, Foreign Military Financing, IMET, Excess Defense Articles, Arms Export Control Act, Security Cooperation (Ch. 16).
Official source: Defense Security Cooperation Agency


Civilian Protection Center of Excellence (Civilian Protection Center)
The Defense Department’s statutory focal point for preventing, mitigating, and responding to civilian harm from U.S. military operations.
Laws in this wiki: Civilian Protection Center, Civilian Casualty Policy, Civilian Casualty Report.
Official source: GovInfo, 10 U.S.C. 184


State Department, Bureau of Political-Military Affairs (State PM bureau)
The State Department’s link to the Defense Department. Leads on security assistance policy, including FMF and peacekeeping funds, and on arms transfer policy; its Directorate of Defense Trade Controls licenses commercial arms exports under the International Traffic in Arms Regulations.
Laws in this wiki: Arms Export Control Act, Foreign Military Financing, Foreign Military Sales, IMET, Peacekeeping Operations.
Official source: Directorate of Defense Trade Controls


Office of the Director of National Intelligence (ODNI)
Created in 2004 to head the intelligence community, a role the CIA director had held. The Director of National Intelligence is the President’s principal intelligence adviser and builds the national intelligence budget.
Laws in this wiki: IRTPA, National Security Act.
Official source: GovInfo, 50 U.S.C. 3023


Central Intelligence Agency (CIA)
Created by the National Security Act of 1947. Collects human intelligence, produces all-source analysis, and conducts covert action on presidential findings reported to the intelligence committees.
Laws in this wiki: National Security Act, CIA Act, Intel Oversight Act, Boland Amendments.
Official source: GovInfo, 50 U.S.C. 3035


National Security Agency (NSA)
The Defense Department’s signals intelligence and cybersecurity agency, established by presidential directive in 1952. Its collection inside the United States and against U.S. persons is governed by FISA.
Laws in this wiki: FISA, FISA Amendments Act (702), USA FREEDOM Act, RISAA.
Official source: National Security Agency


Office of Foreign Assets Control, Department of the Treasury (OFAC)
Administers and enforces most U.S. sanctions programs, including those under IEEPA, and maintains the Specially Designated Nationals list.
Laws in this wiki: IEEPA, Trading with the Enemy Act, Global Magnitsky Act, CAATSA, Helms-Burton Act.
Official source: Office of Foreign Assets Control


Bureau of Industry and Security, Department of Commerce (BIS)
Administers export controls on dual-use and less sensitive military items under the Export Control Reform Act, including the Entity List, and conducts Section 232 investigations.
Laws in this wiki: Export Control Reform Act, Section 232 (trade).
Official source: Bureau of Industry and Security


Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (CFIUS)
The interagency committee, chaired by the Treasury Secretary, that reviews foreign investments in U.S. businesses and real estate for national security risks. FIRRMA widened its reach in 2018.
Laws in this wiki: Defense Production Act, FIRRMA (CFIUS).
Official source: Department of the Treasury, CFIUS


Department of Homeland Security (DHS)
Created in 2002 by combining 22 agencies. Leads on border security, critical infrastructure protection, and civilian cybersecurity through its Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.
Laws in this wiki: Homeland Security Act, Cyber Info Sharing Act.
Official source: GovInfo, 6 U.S.C. 111

Courts 1

Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court (FISC)
Eleven federal district judges designated by the Chief Justice who approve surveillance orders under FISA and review the annual Section 702 certifications. A separate Court of Review hears appeals.
Laws in this wiki: FISA, FISA Amendments Act (702), USA FREEDOM Act, RISAA.
Official source: Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court

title: Unit 3: Deciding to use force
text:
Previous: Unit 2. Building the national security state, 1947 to 1958 | All units | Next: Unit 4. The power of the purse
After Vietnam, Congress tried to rebuild its share of the decision to fight. The War Powers Resolution set a framework of consultation, reports, and a 60-day clock. Every later authorization for use of military force was written to satisfy it. This unit traces the line from the Tonkin Gulf Resolution to the 2001 AUMF, and to the repeal of the two Iraq authorizations in 2025.

title: Unit 3: Deciding to use force
section: What you should be able to do
text:
What you should be able to do

Explain the War Powers Resolution’s reporting requirement and 60-day clock.
Compare the scope of the 1991, 2001, and 2002 authorizations.
Describe how U.N. Security Council mandates relate to congressional authorization.

title: Unit 3: Deciding to use force
text:
Reading path
Read these in order. Each card links to the wiki page and to the official text. Ticking a box saves your progress in this browser only.

War Powers Resolution 1973 In force Framework statute
Passed over President Nixon’s veto, the War Powers Resolution is Congress’s framework statute for sharing the decision to commit U.S. forces to hostilities.
Read it: enacted text, current code  I have read this


Gulf of Tonkin Resolution 1964 Repealed Specific authorization
A joint resolution approving ‘all necessary measures’ by the President to repel attacks on U.S. forces and prevent further aggression in Southeast Asia.
Read it: enacted text  I have read this


1991 Gulf War AUMF 1991 Repealed Specific authorization
Authorized the President to use force under U.N. Security Council Resolution 678 to expel Iraqi forces from Kuwait, after a presidential determination that diplomatic means had been exhausted.
Read it: enacted text, current code  I have read this


2001 AUMF 2001 In force Specific authorization
Enacted a week after the September 11 attacks, this joint resolution authorizes the President to use all necessary and appropriate force against the nations, organizations, or persons that planned, authorized, committed, or aided the attacks, or that harbored those who did.
Read it: enacted text, current code  I have read this


2002 Iraq AUMF 2002 Repealed Specific authorization
Authorized the President to use the armed forces to defend U.S. national security against the continuing threat posed by Iraq and to enforce relevant U.N. Security Council resolutions.
Read it: enacted text, current code  I have read this


UN Participation Act 1945 In force Framework statute
Governs U.S. participation in the United Nations: how representatives are appointed, how the United States carries out Security Council decisions, and the terms on which U.S. forces may be made available to the Council.
Read it: enacted text, current code  I have read this


Court cases

Hamdi 542 U.S. 507 (2004) Court case
The 2001 AUMF authorizes detaining individuals who fought against the United States in Afghanistan as part of or supporting Taliban forces, including citizens, for the duration of the relevant hostilities.
Read it: opinion  I have read this


Hamdan 548 U.S. 557 (2006) Court case
No. The commissions’ procedures violated the Uniform Code of Military Justice, which requires that commission rules match those of courts-martial as far as practicable, and Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions.
Read it: opinion  I have read this


Boumediene 553 U.S. 723 (2008) Court case
Yes, they have the privilege. Sec. 7 of the Military Commissions Act, which stripped federal courts of jurisdiction over their habeas petitions, operates as an unconstitutional suspension of the writ, and the review procedures of the Detainee Treatment Act are not an adequate substitute.
Read it: opinion  I have read this

title: Unit 3: Deciding to use force
text:
Further reading

Case-Zablocki Act: Requires the Secretary of State to send Congress the text of international agreements other than treaties.
Declarations of War: Congress has declared war eleven times, in five conflicts: the War of 1812, the Mexican-American War, the Spanish-American War, and the two world wars.
Constitution (war powers): The Constitution divides national security powers between Congress and the President and leaves the boundary largely undefined.

title: Unit 3: Deciding to use force
text:
Key terms

AUMF

An authorization for use of military force, a joint resolution that gives the President statutory authority to use force for a stated purpose. Modern AUMFs declare themselves the specific authorization the War Powers Resolution requires.

Hostilities

The War Powers Resolution’s trigger term, which it never defines. Most disputes over the resolution turn on whether an operation amounts to hostilities.

60-day clock

Under WPR Sec. 5(b), forces must be withdrawn within 60 days of a required report, plus 30 days for safe withdrawal, unless Congress authorizes the operation.

title: Unit 3: Deciding to use force
text:
Issues for Congress
Questions that recur in oversight and legislation, with the main arguments on each side. There is no answer key; they are for discussion and briefing preparation.

1. Should the 2001 AUMF be repealed, replaced, or left in place?
The 2001 AUMF has no sunset and has been applied to groups that did not exist in 2001.

Advocates of repeal or replacement argue a 2001 authorization should not support operations decades later against new groups, and that a new law should name adversaries, set geographic limits, and include an end date or reporting requirements.
Those who favor keeping it argue its flexibility allows counterterrorism operations against evolving threats, and that a narrower law could leave gaps or signal reduced resolve.



2. Can the War Powers Resolution be made enforceable?
Presidents report ‘consistent with’ the War Powers Resolution rather than under it, and the 60-day clock rarely binds.

Reform proposals would define ‘hostilities,’ tie automatic funding cutoffs to the clock, or strengthen expedited procedures that force votes.
Critics of reform argue the Constitution, not a statute, defines the President’s defensive powers, and that Congress already holds the decisive tool, the power of the purse.



3. Should Congress legislate detention standards rather than leave them to the courts?
Hamdan led to the Military Commissions Act, and Boumediene struck down part of it; detention standards have since been set largely in habeas litigation.

Some argue Congress should set detailed standards for who may be detained and for how long, so that policy is made by statute rather than case by case.
Others argue the current mix of statute, case law, and executive practice is workable, and that new detention legislation risks entrenching indefinite detention.

title: Unit 3: Deciding to use force
text:
Check yourself
Try to answer each question before opening it.






Tip1. What starts the War Powers Resolution’s 60-day clock?





A report under Sec. 4(a)(1), due within 48 hours of introducing forces into hostilities or imminent hostilities. Presidents often file reports ‘consistent with’ the resolution instead, which is why the clock rarely binds. See War Powers Resolution.









Tip2. Whom does the 2001 AUMF authorize force against?





The nations, organizations, or persons the President determines planned, authorized, committed, or aided the September 11 attacks, or harbored those who did. It has no sunset. See 2001 AUMF.









Tip3. What happened to the 1991 and 2002 Iraq authorizations?





Both were repealed by the FY2026 defense authorization in December 2025. See 1991 Gulf War AUMF and 2002 Iraq AUMF.









Tip4. Why was the Tonkin Gulf Resolution’s history central to the War Powers Resolution?





Its open-ended approval of ‘all necessary measures’ became the legal basis for escalating the Vietnam War, and Congress designed the War Powers Resolution to prevent another open-ended grant. See Gulf of Tonkin Resolution.

title: Unit 4: The power of the purse
text:
Previous: Unit 3. Deciding to use force | All units | Next: Unit 5. Emergency and economic powers
An authorization says what the government may do; an appropriation decides whether it can pay for it. Two annual acts, Defense and State-foreign operations, fund nearly everything in this wiki, and their general provisions carry standing policy. Fiscal law, chiefly the Antideficiency Act and the Impoundment Control Act, keeps the executive within the amounts and purposes Congress sets. Funding limits have ended a war and restricted a covert program. This unit covers the vocabulary appropriations staff use every day.

title: Unit 4: The power of the purse
section: What you should be able to do
text:
What you should be able to do

Distinguish an authorization from an appropriation, and explain what happens when only one is enacted.
Explain apportionment, transfer, reprogramming, rescission, and deferral.
Describe how Congress has used funding limits to end or restrict operations.
Explain what the Impoundment Control Act requires and how it has been tested since 2025.

title: Unit 4: The power of the purse
text:
Reading path
Read these in order. Each card links to the wiki page and to the official text. Ticking a box saves your progress in this browser only.

Defense appropriations (annual) 1949 In force Specific authorization
The annual law that provides the Defense Department’s money. The NDAA sets policy and authorizes amounts; this act makes funds available to obligate, account by account, and attaches general provisions that limit how they may be used.
Read it: enacted text  I have read this


State-foreign ops appropriations 1961 In force Specific authorization
The annual law that funds the State Department and foreign assistance, including the security assistance accounts that pay for Foreign Military Financing, IMET, and Peacekeeping Operations.
Read it: enacted text  I have read this


Antideficiency Act 1905 In force Framework statute
The fiscal law that makes the purse enforceable. Federal officials may not spend or obligate more than Congress has appropriated, may not commit the government to pay before an appropriation is made, and may not accept voluntary services.
Read it: enacted text, current code  I have read this


Impoundment Control Act 1974 In force Framework statute
Title X of the Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act of 1974. It requires the President to spend appropriated funds unless Congress agrees otherwise.
Read it: enacted text, current code  I have read this


Sec. 8005 transfers 2026 In force Targeted provision
The recurring section of the annual Defense appropriations act that lets the Secretary of Defense, with the approval of the Director of the Office of Management and Budget, move funds between accounts up to a cap set each year ($6 billion for fiscal 2026).
Read it: enacted text  I have read this


Coup restriction (Sec. 7008) 2026 In force Targeted provision
Bars the use of foreign assistance funds to finance assistance directly to the government of a country whose duly elected head of government is deposed by a military coup or decree, or by a coup or decree in which the military plays a decisive role.
Read it: enacted text  I have read this


Case-Church Amendment 1973 Lapsed Targeted provision
The funding cutoff that ended U.S. combat in Indochina. Section 307 of the Second Supplemental Appropriations Act, 1973 barred the use of its funds to support, directly or indirectly, combat by U.S. forces in or over Cambodia, Laos, North Vietnam, and South Vietnam or off their shores, and barred any previously appropriated funds for that purpose after August 15, 1973.
Read it: enacted text  I have read this


Boland Amendments 1982 Lapsed Targeted provision
A series of appropriations limits on U.S. support for the Contras fighting Nicaragua’s government.
Read it: enacted text  I have read this


Court cases

Train v. New York 420 U.S. 35 (1975) Court case
No. The statute required the Administrator to allot the full sums authorized; he had no discretion to withhold them.
Read it: opinion  I have read this

title: Unit 4: The power of the purse
text:
Further reading

NDAA (annual): The annual law that authorizes funding levels and sets policy for the Defense Department and the nuclear weapons programs of the Energy Department.
Constitution (war powers): The Constitution divides national security powers between Congress and the President and leaves the boundary largely undefined.
Section 2808 (construction): One of the standby powers unlocked by a national emergency. When a declared war or emergency requires use of the armed forces, the Secretary of Defense may build military construction projects that Congress never authorized, using unspent military construction funds.
Section 284 (counterdrug): Authorizes the Defense Department to support the counterdrug and counter transnational organized crime work of other federal agencies and of state, local, and foreign law enforcement, when they ask for it.
CIA Act: Gave the CIA the administrative tools to operate in secret: authority to spend money without the usual accounting rules, to withhold information about its staff and structure, and to procure and transfer funds confidentially.

title: Unit 4: The power of the purse
text:
Key terms

Authorization

A law that establishes or continues an agency or program and may recommend funding levels, but does not itself provide money.

Appropriation

Budget authority provided by law to incur obligations and make payments for specified purposes. No money may be drawn from the Treasury without one.

Obligation

A binding commitment, such as a contract or grant, that will require a payment. The Antideficiency Act bars obligations beyond, or in advance of, an appropriation.

Apportionment

The Office of Management and Budget’s division of an appropriation by time period or project, which agencies need before they may obligate funds.

Transfer

Moving budget authority from one appropriation account to another. Allowed only when a statute authorizes it, as Sec. 8005 does for the Defense Department.

Reprogramming

Shifting funds within an account from one purpose to another, governed mainly by notification to the Appropriations Committees rather than by statute.

Rescission

A law cancelling budget authority before it is obligated. The President may propose one under the Impoundment Control Act.

Deferral

A temporary withholding of funds, allowed under the Impoundment Control Act only for limited reasons and not past the end of the fiscal year.

Continuing resolution

A joint resolution that funds agencies, usually at the prior year’s rate, when regular appropriations are not enacted. It generally bars new programs and production increases.

title: Unit 4: The power of the purse
text:
Issues for Congress
Questions that recur in oversight and legislation, with the main arguments on each side. There is no answer key; they are for discussion and briefing preparation.

1. Should Congress rely more on funding limits to check the use of force?
The Case-Church Amendment and the Boland Amendments limited operations through appropriations, and recent bills propose barring funds for military action against specific countries.

Supporters argue the purse is Congress’s clearest constitutional check and is harder for the executive to work around than the War Powers Resolution.
Critics argue funding cutoffs are blunt, can endanger forces already deployed, and, since they must be enacted like any law, rarely survive a veto.



2. How should Congress respond to impoundments and pocket rescissions?
Since 2025 the Impoundment Control Act has been tested by an enacted rescission of foreign assistance and by a pocket rescission that let funds expire.

Some propose tightening the act, for example by barring rescission proposals late in the fiscal year or adding enforcement tools and reporting requirements.
Others argue the President needs room to avoid wasteful spending and that the act already provides the right channel, an enacted rescission, for doing so with Congress’s consent.



3. How much transfer and reprogramming flexibility should the Defense Department have?
Sec. 8005 transfers caps general transfers each year and bars using them for items Congress denied.

Those favoring more flexibility argue that a budget prepared nearly two years before execution cannot anticipate every need, and that larger transfer authority supports faster response.
Those favoring tighter limits argue broad transfer authority weakens Congress’s control over specific programs, and point to the 2019 border barrier transfers as an example.

title: Unit 4: The power of the purse
text:
Check yourself
Try to answer each question before opening it.






Tip1. What is the difference between the NDAA and the Defense appropriations act?





The NDAA (annual) authorizes programs, sets policy, and recommends funding levels. The Defense appropriations (annual) provides the budget authority the Defense Department can actually obligate. An authorized program with no appropriation spends nothing.









Tip2. What does the Antideficiency Act prohibit, and why does it matter in a shutdown?





It bars obligating or spending more than, or before, Congress appropriates, and accepting voluntary services. When appropriations lapse, agencies must stop work except where law allows it, such as emergencies involving the safety of human life or the protection of property. See Antideficiency Act.









Tip3. How did Congress end U.S. combat in Indochina?





With the Case-Church Amendment, a section of a 1973 supplemental appropriations act that barred funds for U.S. combat in or over Cambodia, Laos, North Vietnam, and South Vietnam after August 15, 1973.









Tip4. What happens to funds the President proposes to rescind?





Under the Impoundment Control Act, the President sends Congress a special message and may withhold the funds for 45 days of continuous session; they must then be released unless Congress has enacted a rescission bill. A proposal sent late in the fiscal year, a pocket rescission, can let the funds expire, which GAO has said the act does not permit.

title: Unit 9: The military at home
text:
Previous: Unit 8. Organizing and commanding the military | All units | Next: Unit 10. Foreign assistance, fragility, and partners
The default rule is that federal troops do not enforce civilian law. The Posse Comitatus Act states the rule; the Insurrection Act is the main exception. Whether the rule applies often turns on the National Guard’s status: under governor control in Title 32 or federalized under Title 10. Counterdrug support and mobilization authorities fill in the rest.

title: Unit 9: The military at home
text:
Reading path
Read these in order. Each card links to the wiki page and to the official text. Ticking a box saves your progress in this browser only.

Posse Comitatus Act 1878 In force Framework statute
A one-sentence criminal statute that bars using federal military forces to execute the laws unless the Constitution or an act of Congress expressly authorizes it.
Read it: enacted text, current code  I have read this


Insurrection Act 1807 In force Framework statute
A set of provisions, first enacted in 1807 and broadened in 1861 and 1871, that lets the President use the armed forces and federalized militia inside the United States to suppress insurrection, enforce federal law, or protect civil rights when ordinary enforcement fails.
Read it: enacted text, current code  I have read this


Reserve & Guard Mobilization 1952 In force Framework statute
The set of Title 10 provisions, descended from the Armed Forces Reserve Act of 1952 and earlier militia acts, that let the federal government order reserve forces and the National Guard to active duty.
Read it: enacted text, current code  I have read this


Militia Act of 1903 1903 Superseded Framework statute
Replaced the 1792 militia system. It divided the militia into an organized part, the National Guard, and an unorganized reserve, and gave the Guard federal funding and equipment in exchange for meeting Army standards.
Read it: enacted text, current code  I have read this


National Defense Act (1916) 1916 Superseded Framework statute
The first comprehensive statute organizing U.S. land forces. It defined the Army as the Regular Army, the National Guard, and a federal reserve, and it let the President draft the Guard into federal service for use overseas.
Read it: enacted text, current code  I have read this


Section 284 (counterdrug) 1990 In force Targeted provision
Authorizes the Defense Department to support the counterdrug and counter transnational organized crime work of other federal agencies and of state, local, and foreign law enforcement, when they ask for it.
Read it: enacted text, current code  I have read this

title: Unit 9: The military at home
text:
Further reading

Militia Acts of 1792: Two acts passed a week apart. The first let the President call out state militias to repel invasion, suppress insurrection, and enforce federal law.
Title 32 U.S.C.: The title of the U.S. Code for the National Guard when it is not in federal service. It governs organization, federal funding, and training of the Guard while it remains under the command of state governors.
Homeland Security Act: Created the Department of Homeland Security by merging 22 agencies, the largest federal reorganization since 1947.
Alien Enemies Act: The only one of the Alien and Sedition Acts still in force. During a declared war, or an invasion or predatory incursion by a foreign nation or government, the President may detain, restrict, and remove nationals of the hostile country.

title: Unit 9: The military at home
text:
Key terms

Title 32 status

National Guard duty under the command of a state governor, often with federal funding. Posse Comitatus does not apply.

Federalization

Ordering Guard members into federal service under Title 10, which places them under the President and within Posse Comitatus limits unless an exception applies.

title: Unit 9: The military at home
text:
Issues for Congress
Questions that recur in oversight and legislation, with the main arguments on each side. There is no answer key; they are for discussion and briefing preparation.

1. Should the Insurrection Act be narrowed?
The Insurrection Act lets the President use the military domestically on broad and largely undefined conditions.

Reform proposals would define the triggering conditions, require consultation with or approval by Congress after a set period, and provide for judicial review.
Opponents argue the President needs flexibility in genuine emergencies and that new limits could delay a response when state authorities cannot or will not act.



2. Where should the line fall between federal and state control of the National Guard?
A Guard member’s status under the mobilization authorities decides whether the Posse Comitatus Act applies.

Some argue for clearer limits on federalizing a state’s Guard over the governor’s objection.
Others argue federal authority must remain available to enforce federal law and protect federal functions.

title: Unit 9: The military at home
text:
Check yourself
Try to answer each question before opening it.






Tip1. What does the Posse Comitatus Act prohibit?





Using federal military forces to execute the laws unless the Constitution or an act of Congress expressly authorizes it. See Posse Comitatus Act.









Tip2. What is the principal statutory exception to Posse Comitatus?





The Insurrection Act, which lets the President use the armed forces and federalized militia to suppress insurrection, enforce federal law, or protect civil rights when ordinary enforcement fails.









Tip3. What did the Dick Act do to the old militia system?





It divided the militia into an organized part, the National Guard, and an unorganized reserve, and gave the Guard federal funds and equipment in exchange for meeting Army standards. See Militia Act of 1903.









Tip4. Why does a Guard member’s duty status matter?





Under Title 32 the Guard serves the governor and Posse Comitatus does not apply; federalized under Title 10, it does unless an exception applies. See Reserve & Guard Mobilization and Title 32 U.S.C..

Every statute in this wiki rests on a handful of clauses in Articles I and II. Congress holds the war, money, and military-rulemaking powers; the President is commander in chief and conducts diplomacy. The founding-era statutes show Congress using those powers early: calling out the militia, policing private war-making, and controlling enemy aliens. title: Unit 1: Where the power comes from
text:
Key terms

Positive law title

A U.S. Code title Congress has itself enacted, so the Code text is the law. Titles 10 and 32 are positive law; Titles 22 and 50 are not, so for them the Statutes at Large control.

Statutes at Large

The official chronological publication of every law as enacted, cited by volume and page, for example 87 Stat. 555.

Declaration of war

A joint resolution or act under Article I declaring that a state of war exists. Congress has passed eleven, in five wars, the last in 1942.

title: Unit 1: Where the power comes from
text:
Issues for Congress
Questions that recur in oversight and legislation, with the main arguments on each side. There is no answer key; they are for discussion and briefing preparation.

1. Should Congress return to formal declarations of war, or keep relying on authorizations for use of force?
Congress has not declared war since 1942 (Declarations of War); statutory authorizations now do that work.

Proponents of declarations argue they force a clear, accountable decision and carry legal consequences, such as triggering the Alien Enemies Act, that authorizations do not.
Others argue declarations fit wars between states, not operations against non-state groups, and that tailored authorizations can set purpose, scope, and duration more precisely.



2. How much deference should Congress give the executive in foreign affairs?
Curtiss-Wright and Zivotofsky v. Kerry point in different directions on the reach of the President’s foreign affairs power.

Those favoring deference cite the need for speed, secrecy, and a single voice abroad, and the President’s recognition and diplomatic powers.
Those favoring a stronger congressional role cite Congress’s Article I powers over war, commerce, and money, and Justice Jackson’s point that presidential power is weakest when it runs against Congress.

title: Unit 1: Where the power comes from
text:
Check yourself
Try to answer each question before opening it.






Tip1. Which branch holds the power to declare war, and which commands the forces once committed?





Congress declares war, raises and supports armies, provides a navy, and makes rules for the forces under Article I, Section 8; the President is commander in chief under Article II. The Constitution (war powers) page lays out the clauses and the undefined ground between them.









Tip2. How many declarations of war has Congress passed, and in which conflicts?





Eleven, in five conflicts, from the War of 1812 through the Second World War. See Declarations of War. Later conflicts were fought under statutory authorizations instead.









Tip3. Which of the Alien and Sedition Acts is still in force, and what triggers it?





The Alien Enemies Act. It applies during a declared war or an invasion or predatory incursion by a foreign nation or government, and lets the President detain, restrict, and remove nationals of the hostile country.









Tip4. Why does it matter whether a U.S. Code title is positive law?





In a positive law title, such as Title 10, the Code text is the law itself. In a non-positive title such as Title 50, the Code is only evidence of the law, and the enacted text in the Statutes at Large controls if they differ.

Further reading

DoD Reorganization Act (1958): President Eisenhower’s reorganization. It took the military departments out of the operational chain of command, so that orders run from the President and the Secretary of Defense to unified commands, and it confirmed the Secretary’s authority, direction, and control over the whole department.
Security Cooperation (Ch. 16): The FY2017 defense authorization gathered dozens of scattered Defense Department authorities for training, equipping, and advising foreign forces into a single chapter of Title 10, with common definitions, oversight, and evaluation rules.

title: Unit 8: Organizing and commanding the military
text:
Key terms

Combatant commander

The commander of a unified combatant command, who receives operational orders from the President through the Secretary of Defense.

Surrogate force

A foreign force supporting U.S. special operations toward U.S. objectives, funded under 10 U.S.C. 127e, as distinct from a partner force built up for its own missions.

Traditional military activity

A military operation outside the covert action definition. Section 394 classifies clandestine military cyber activity this way.

title: Unit 8: Organizing and commanding the military
text:
Issues for Congress
Questions that recur in oversight and legislation, with the main arguments on each side. There is no answer key; they are for discussion and briefing preparation.

1. Has the annual NDAA become too large a vehicle?
The NDAA (annual) routinely carries legislation well beyond defense policy.

Defenders say its must-pass status is what lets Congress complete national security legislation every year.
Critics argue the practice reduces scrutiny of attached measures and concentrates power in the final negotiations between the committees.



2. Is it time to revisit Goldwater-Nichols?
The Goldwater-Nichols Act set the balance between the services, the Joint Staff, and the combatant commands.

Reformers point to joint requirements, acquisition, and the relationship between the services and the combatant commands as unfinished business.
Others credit the act with the joint force’s effectiveness and warn against large changes without clear evidence of the problem.

title: Unit 8: Organizing and commanding the military
text:
Check yourself
Try to answer each question before opening it.






Tip1. Under Goldwater-Nichols, who is the principal military adviser to the President?





The Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff. The act also ran the chain of command from the President through the Secretary of Defense to the combatant commanders. See Goldwater-Nichols Act.









Tip2. What did the Nunn-Cohen Amendment create?





U.S. Special Operations Command, with its own budget line and a civilian assistant secretary for oversight. See Nunn-Cohen Amendment.









Tip3. What does Section 2808 allow during a declared national emergency?





If the emergency requires use of the armed forces, the Secretary of Defense may undertake military construction Congress never authorized, using unspent military construction funds. See Section 2808 (construction).









Tip4. Why does so much national security law ride on the NDAA?





It has been enacted every year for more than six decades, so it is the most reliable vehicle for legislation of all kinds. See NDAA (annual).

The Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 is the base law of foreign aid, run largely by the State Department. The Defense Department has its own parallel set of authorities for training and equipping foreign forces, consolidated in Title 10 Chapter 16. IMET and Peacekeeping Operations show the State Department side in practice. Conditions such as the Leahy Laws attach to both, and the annual appropriations act adds more, such as the coup restriction. The Global Fragility Act, the Women, Peace, and Security Act, and the Elie Wiesel Act direct strategy toward conflict prevention.

title: Unit 10: Foreign assistance, fragility, and partners
text:
Further reading

Coup restriction (Sec. 7008): Bars the use of foreign assistance funds to finance assistance directly to the government of a country whose duly elected head of government is deposed by a military coup or decree, or by a coup or decree in which the military plays a decisive role.
Presidential drawdown (Sec. 506): Lets the President send weapons, equipment, services, and training from existing Defense Department stocks to a foreign country in an emergency or for listed purposes, without a new appropriation.
Millennium Challenge Act: Created the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a small government corporation that gives large, multi-year grants to poor countries that pass a scorecard of governance, economic freedom, and social investment indicators.
Foreign Affairs Reform Act: Division G of the FY1999 omnibus appropriations act. It folded the Arms Control and Disarmament Agency and the U.S. Information Agency into the State Department and, for the first time, gave USAID a statutory existence as an independent establishment.
State Basic Authorities Act: The organic statute of the State Department. It sets out the Secretary’s management authorities, the department’s senior positions, and a long list of operating powers that have been added over the decades.
Foreign Service Act: The personnel law for U.S. diplomats. It establishes a career Foreign Service based on merit, with rank held by the person and not the job, competitive promotion, and worldwide availability.
Nunn-Lugar Act: Authorized the Defense Department to spend its own funds helping the former Soviet republics secure, transport, and dismantle nuclear, chemical, and other weapons after the Soviet collapse.
Mutual Security Act: Merged the Marshall Plan’s economic aid, military assistance to allies, and technical assistance into one program under one agency, with the stated purpose of strengthening the free world against Soviet power.
Smith-Mundt Act: The legal foundation of U.S. public diplomacy. It authorized the State Department to explain the United States to foreign audiences through broadcasting, publications, and educational and cultural exchanges.

title: Unit 10: Foreign assistance, fragility, and partners
text:
Key terms

Security cooperation

Defense Department activities with foreign security forces, such as training, equipping, and advising, mostly under Title 10 Chapter 16.

Security assistance

Programs under Title 22, run by the State Department, that provide defense articles, training, and services to foreign governments.

Leahy vetting

Screening foreign security force units for credible information of gross violations of human rights before they receive U.S. assistance.

Security assistance

Programs authorized mainly in Title 22 and funded in the State-foreign operations act, under State Department policy direction, such as FMF, IMET, and Peacekeeping Operations.

Security cooperation

Defense Department activities with foreign forces under Title 10, consolidated in Chapter 16 in 2016, and overseen by the armed services committees.

title: Unit 10: Foreign assistance, fragility, and partners
text:
Issues for Congress
Questions that recur in oversight and legislation, with the main arguments on each side. There is no answer key; they are for discussion and briefing preparation.

1. Should Congress rewrite the Foreign Assistance Act?
The Foreign Assistance Act has been amended for more than six decades, and much aid policy is now set in the annual appropriations act.

Supporters of a rewrite argue the act is outdated and layered with amendments, and that appropriations riders have become a substitute for authorization.
Skeptics argue a rewrite is unlikely to pass and could invite cuts, while the current system lets Congress adjust policy every year.



2. Should security assistance stop after a coup?
The coup restriction cuts off most assistance to a government installed by coup; recent acts added a national security waiver.

Those favoring strict application argue cutting aid upholds democratic norms and U.S. credibility.
Those favoring flexibility argue ending security ties can cede influence to rivals and harm counterterrorism cooperation.
