title: Timeline
text: Each generation of national security law answered the problems of the one before. Read an era’s entries together to see the pattern: a crisis, a grant of power, and later a constraint, often prompted by a court decision. Dates are years of enactment or decision; for code-title and annual-series entries they are the year the title or series began. Court cases are shaded.

title: Timeline
text:
Founding and the early republic



1788


U.S. Constitution: War and Foreign Affairs Powers In force Constitution

The Constitution divides national security powers between Congress and the President and leaves the boundary largely undefined.





1792


Militia Acts of 1792 Superseded Framework statute

Two acts passed a week apart. The first let the President call out state militias to repel invasion, suppress insurrection, and enforce federal law.





1794


Neutrality Act of 1794 In force Framework statute

Makes it a crime for private persons to wage war from U.S. territory against a country with which the United States is at peace.





1798


Alien Enemies Act of 1798 In force Framework statute

The only one of the Alien and Sedition Acts still in force. During a declared war, or an invasion or predatory incursion by a foreign nation or government, the President may detain, restrict, and remove nationals of the hostile country.





1799


Logan Act In force Targeted provision

Bars private citizens from corresponding with a foreign government, without authority, in order to influence its conduct in a dispute with the United States or to defeat U.S. measures.





1807


Insurrection Act In force Framework statute

A set of provisions, first enacted in 1807 and broadened in 1861 and 1871, that lets the President use the armed forces and federalized militia inside the United States to suppress insurrection, enforce federal law, or protect civil rights when ordinary enforcement fails.





1812


Declarations of War (1812-1942) In force Specific authorization

Congress has declared war eleven times, in five conflicts: the War of 1812, the Mexican-American War, the Spanish-American War, and the two world wars.

title: Timeline
section: Civil War to the First World War
text:
Civil War to the First World War



1878


Posse Comitatus Act In force Framework statute

A one-sentence criminal statute that bars using federal military forces to execute the laws unless the Constitution or an act of Congress expressly authorizes it.





1903


Militia Act of 1903 (Dick Act) Superseded Framework statute

Replaced the 1792 militia system. It divided the militia into an organized part, the National Guard, and an unorganized reserve, and gave the Guard federal funding and equipment in exchange for meeting Army standards.





1905


Antideficiency Act In force Framework statute

The fiscal law that makes the purse enforceable. Federal officials may not spend or obligate more than Congress has appropriated, may not commit the government to pay before an appropriation is made, and may not accept voluntary services.





1916


National Defense Act of 1916 Superseded Framework statute

The first comprehensive statute organizing U.S. land forces. It defined the Army as the Regular Army, the National Guard, and a federal reserve, and it let the President draft the Guard into federal service for use overseas.





1917


Espionage Act of 1917 In force Framework statute

The principal criminal statute protecting national defense information. It covers classic spying for a foreign power and also the unauthorized retention or disclosure of defense information by people who had lawful access to it.





1917


Trading with the Enemy Act of 1917 In force Framework statute

A First World War statute giving the President sweeping control over trade and property involving enemy countries and nationals.

title: Timeline
section: Interwar years and the Second World War
text:
Interwar years and the Second World War



1926


Title 22, U.S. Code: Foreign Relations and Intercourse In force Code title overview

The title of the U.S. Code for diplomacy and foreign assistance. It holds the State Department’s authorities, the Foreign Service, foreign aid, arms export controls, and most country-specific sanctions and policy statutes.





1926


Title 50, U.S. Code: War and National Defense In force Code title overview

The title of the U.S. Code that collects the laws on war powers, emergency powers, intelligence, and economic defense.





1936


United States v. Curtiss-Wright Export Corp., 299 U.S. 304 Supreme Court

Upheld the delegation. Because foreign affairs powers rest on national sovereignty rather than on the Constitution’s specific grants alone, Congress may give the President broader discretion abroad than at home.





1938


Foreign Agents Registration Act of 1938 In force Framework statute

A disclosure law. People who act in the United States on behalf of foreign governments, parties, or other foreign principals in political or public relations work must register with the Justice Department and report their activities and payments.





1941


Lend-Lease Act Superseded Specific authorization

Authorized the President to sell, transfer, lend, or lease defense articles to any country whose defense he judged vital to the defense of the United States.





1942


Foreign Claims Act In force Targeted provision

Lets the military departments appoint claims commissions to settle claims by inhabitants of foreign countries for property loss, injury, or death caused by U.S. forces or incident to their noncombat activities abroad.





1945


United Nations Participation Act of 1945 In force Framework statute

Governs U.S. participation in the United Nations: how representatives are appointed, how the United States carries out Security Council decisions, and the terms on which U.S. forces may be made available to the Council.

title: Timeline
text:
Building the national security state



1947


National Security Act of 1947 In force Framework statute

The founding charter of the modern national security system. It created the National Security Council and the Central Intelligence Agency, established a separate Air Force, and placed the military departments under a single Secretary of Defense.





1948


Military Selective Service Act Partly expired Framework statute

The standing law of conscription. It requires men to register at 18 and maintains the Selective Service System so that a draft could be run if Congress and the President restored the power to induct.





1948


U.S. Information and Educational Exchange Act of 1948 (Smith-Mundt) In force Framework statute

The legal foundation of U.S. public diplomacy. It authorized the State Department to explain the United States to foreign audiences through broadcasting, publications, and educational and cultural exchanges.





1949


Central Intelligence Agency Act of 1949 In force Framework statute

Gave the CIA the administrative tools to operate in secret: authority to spend money without the usual accounting rules, to withhold information about its staff and structure, and to procure and transfer funds confidentially.





1949


Department of Defense Appropriations Act (annual series) In force Specific authorization

The annual law that provides the Defense Department’s money. The NDAA sets policy and authorizes amounts; this act makes funds available to obligate, account by account, and attaches general provisions that limit how they may be used.





1949


National Security Act Amendments of 1949 In force Framework statute

Fixed the weak structure created in 1947. It turned the National Military Establishment into the Department of Defense, an executive department, and reduced the Army, Navy, and Air Force to military departments under the Secretary of Defense.





1950


Defense Production Act of 1950 Partly expired Framework statute

A Korean War statute that lets the President direct private industry in the interest of national defense: by putting government orders first in line, by financing new production capacity, and by organizing industry cooperation.





1950


Uniform Code of Military Justice In force Framework statute

The criminal code and court system of the U.S. armed forces. It replaced the separate Army and Navy disciplinary codes with one law for all services, defining military offenses, the types of courts-martial, the rights of the accused, and civilian appellate review.





1951


Mutual Security Act of 1951 Superseded Specific authorization

Merged the Marshall Plan’s economic aid, military assistance to allies, and technical assistance into one program under one agency, with the stated purpose of strengthening the free world against Soviet power.





1952


Reserve and National Guard Mobilization Authorities In force Framework statute

The set of Title 10 provisions, descended from the Armed Forces Reserve Act of 1952 and earlier militia acts, that let the federal government order reserve forces and the National Guard to active duty.





1952


Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer, 343 U.S. 579 Supreme Court

Held the seizure unlawful. No statute authorized it, and the President’s powers as Commander in Chief and chief executive did not extend to taking private property at home to settle a labor dispute; that was lawmaking reserved to Congress.





1954


Atomic Energy Act of 1954 In force Framework statute

The governing law for both civilian and military uses of nuclear material in the United States.





1956


State Department Basic Authorities Act of 1956 In force Framework statute

The organic statute of the State Department. It sets out the Secretary’s management authorities, the department’s senior positions, and a long list of operating powers that have been added over the decades.





1956


Title 10, U.S. Code: Armed Forces In force Code title overview

The title of the U.S. Code that governs the armed forces: their organization, command, personnel, training, procurement, and reserve components.





1956


Title 32, U.S. Code: National Guard In force Code title overview

The title of the U.S. Code for the National Guard when it is not in federal service. It governs organization, federal funding, and training of the Guard while it remains under the command of state governors.





1958


Department of Defense Reorganization Act of 1958 In force Framework statute

President Eisenhower’s reorganization. It took the military departments out of the operational chain of command, so that orders run from the President and the Secretary of Defense to unified commands, and it confirmed the Secretary’s authority, direction, and control over the whole department.





1961


Foreign Assistance Act of 1961 In force Framework statute

The basic law of U.S. foreign aid. It separated economic from military assistance, set the purposes and conditions of each, and led President Kennedy to create the U.S. Agency for International Development by executive order two months later.





1961


National Defense Authorization Act (annual series) In force Specific authorization

The annual law that authorizes funding levels and sets policy for the Defense Department and the nuclear weapons programs of the Energy Department.





1961


Presidential Drawdown Authority (Foreign Assistance Act, Sec. 506) In force Targeted provision

Lets the President send weapons, equipment, services, and training from existing Defense Department stocks to a foreign country in an emergency or for listed purposes, without a new appropriation.





1961


State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs Appropriations Act (annual series) In force Specific authorization

The annual law that funds the State Department and foreign assistance, including the security assistance accounts that pay for Foreign Military Financing, IMET, and Peacekeeping Operations.





1962


Trade Expansion Act of 1962, Section 232 In force Targeted provision

Allows the President to restrict imports that threaten to impair national security. The Commerce Department investigates and reports, and the President then decides whether to impose tariffs, quotas, or negotiated limits.

title: Timeline
text:
Vietnam, Watergate, and reassertion



1964


Gulf of Tonkin Resolution Repealed Specific authorization

A joint resolution approving ‘all necessary measures’ by the President to repel attacks on U.S. forces and prevent further aggression in Southeast Asia.





1968


Foreign Military Financing (Arms Export Control Act, Sec. 23) In force Targeted provision

The main U.S. program that pays for foreign governments’ purchases of American weapons, services, and training.





1968


Foreign Military Sales (Arms Export Control Act, Secs. 21-22) In force Targeted provision

The government-to-government channel for selling U.S. defense articles, services, and training.





1972


Case-Zablocki Act In force Targeted provision

Requires the Secretary of State to send Congress the text of international agreements other than treaties.





1973


Case-Church Amendment Lapsed Targeted provision

The funding cutoff that ended U.S. combat in Indochina. Section 307 of the Second Supplemental Appropriations Act, 1973 barred the use of its funds to support, directly or indirectly, combat by U.S. forces in or over Cambodia, Laos, North Vietnam, and South Vietnam or off their shores, and barred any previously appropriated funds for that purpose after August 15, 1973.





1973


War Powers Resolution In force Framework statute

Passed over President Nixon’s veto, the War Powers Resolution is Congress’s framework statute for sharing the decision to commit U.S. forces to hostilities.





1974


Hughes-Ryan Amendment Superseded Targeted provision

Section 32 of the Foreign Assistance Act of 1974, which added section 662 to the Foreign Assistance Act of 1961.





1974


Impoundment Control Act of 1974 In force Framework statute

Title X of the Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act of 1974. It requires the President to spend appropriated funds unless Congress agrees otherwise.





1975


Train v. City of New York, 420 U.S. 35 Supreme Court

No. The statute required the Administrator to allot the full sums authorized; he had no discretion to withhold them.





1976


Arms Export Control Act In force Framework statute

Governs U.S. arms exports. It sets the purposes for which American weapons may be sold, requires licenses for commercial sales, and gives Congress advance notice of major sales and a procedure to block them.





1976


International Military Education and Training (Foreign Assistance Act, Sec. 541) In force Targeted provision

Grant-funded professional military education and training, in the United States and abroad, for foreign military personnel and related civilians.





1976


National Emergencies Act In force Framework statute

Ended the open-ended emergencies that had accumulated since the 1930s and set procedures for declaring, renewing, and terminating national emergencies.





1976


Symington and Glenn Amendments In force Targeted provision

Two nonproliferation amendments from 1976 and 1977 that cut off U.S. economic and military aid to countries that trade in nuclear enrichment or reprocessing technology outside international safeguards, or that test a nuclear device.





1977


International Emergency Economic Powers Act In force Framework statute

The workhorse of U.S. economic sanctions. After declaring a national emergency over an unusual and extraordinary threat that originates largely abroad, the President may block property and prohibit transactions involving foreign countries, entities, and individuals.





1978


Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978 Partly expired Framework statute

Created a judicial process for foreign intelligence surveillance inside the United States.





1978


Peacekeeping Operations (Foreign Assistance Act, Sec. 551) In force Targeted provision

Authority to assist friendly countries and international organizations with peacekeeping operations and other programs that serve U.S. national security interests.





1979


Taiwan Relations Act In force Specific authorization

Passed after the United States recognized the People’s Republic of China and ended formal relations with Taipei.





1980


Classified Information Procedures Act In force Framework statute

Sets pretrial and trial procedures for handling classified information in federal criminal cases, so that a defendant cannot force the government to choose between dropping the case and disclosing secrets.





1980


Foreign Service Act of 1980 In force Framework statute

The personnel law for U.S. diplomats. It establishes a career Foreign Service based on merit, with rank held by the person and not the job, competitive promotion, and worldwide availability.





1980


Intelligence Oversight Act of 1980 In force Framework statute

Enacted as part of the FY1981 intelligence authorization, it added the oversight title to the National Security Act.

title: Timeline
text:
End of the Cold War



1981


Dames & Moore v. Regan, 453 U.S. 654 Supreme Court

Yes. IEEPA authorized nullifying the attachments and transferring the assets. No statute expressly authorized suspending the claims, but Congress’s long acquiescence in executive settlement of international claims, and related statutes, supported the President’s action.





1982


Boland Amendments Lapsed Targeted provision

A series of appropriations limits on U.S. support for the Contras fighting Nicaragua’s government.





1982


Emergency Military Construction Authority (10 U.S.C. 2808) In force Targeted provision

One of the standby powers unlocked by a national emergency. When a declared war or emergency requires use of the armed forces, the Secretary of Defense may build military construction projects that Congress never authorized, using unspent military construction funds.





1983


Immigration and Naturalization Service v. Chadha, 462 U.S. 919 Supreme Court

No. Action with the effect of law must pass both houses and be presented to the President.





1986


Excess Defense Articles (Foreign Assistance Act, Sec. 516) In force Targeted provision

Allows the President to transfer surplus U.S. military equipment to eligible countries, by grant or sale, from existing Defense Department stocks.





1986


Goldwater-Nichols Department of Defense Reorganization Act of 1986 In force Framework statute

The most important reorganization of the Defense Department since 1947. It took operational control away from the service chiefs, ran the chain of command from the President through the Secretary of Defense to the combatant commanders, and made the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs the principal military adviser.





1986


Nunn-Cohen Amendment In force Framework statute

Section 1311 of the FY1987 defense authorization. It created U.S. Special Operations Command as a unified combatant command with its own budget line and a civilian assistant secretary to oversee it.





1990


Defense Support for Counterdrug Activities (10 U.S.C. 284) In force Targeted provision

Authorizes the Defense Department to support the counterdrug and counter transnational organized crime work of other federal agencies and of state, local, and foreign law enforcement, when they ask for it.





1991


Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq Resolution (1991) Repealed Specific authorization

Authorized the President to use force under U.N. Security Council Resolution 678 to expel Iraqi forces from Kuwait, after a presidential determination that diplomatic means had been exhausted.





1991


Soviet Nuclear Threat Reduction Act of 1991 (Nunn-Lugar) In force Specific authorization

Authorized the Defense Department to spend its own funds helping the former Soviet republics secure, transport, and dismantle nuclear, chemical, and other weapons after the Soviet collapse.





1996


Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996 In force Specific authorization

Passed after the Oklahoma City bombing. Its national security significance lies in two linked provisions: the Secretary of State’s power to designate foreign terrorist organizations, and the crime of giving such organizations material support.





1996


Cuban Liberty and Democratic Solidarity (LIBERTAD) Act of 1996 In force Specific authorization

Wrote the Cuba embargo into statute so that a President cannot lift it alone, and extended its reach to foreign companies that use property confiscated by the Cuban government.





1996


Iran Sanctions Act of 1996 In force Specific authorization

Originally the Iran and Libya Sanctions Act. It pioneered secondary sanctions by penalizing foreign companies, not just U.S. ones, that invest in Iran’s energy sector.





1997


Leahy Laws In force Targeted provision

Two parallel provisions that bar U.S. assistance to any unit of a foreign security force when there is credible information that the unit committed a gross violation of human rights.





1998


Foreign Affairs Reform and Restructuring Act of 1998 In force Framework statute

Division G of the FY1999 omnibus appropriations act. It folded the Arms Control and Disarmament Agency and the U.S. Information Agency into the State Department and, for the first time, gave USAID a statutory existence as an independent establishment.

title: Timeline
text:
After September 11



2001


Authorization for Use of Military Force (2001) In force Specific authorization

Enacted a week after the September 11 attacks, this joint resolution authorizes the President to use all necessary and appropriate force against the nations, organizations, or persons that planned, authorized, committed, or aided the attacks, or that harbored those who did.





2001


USA PATRIOT Act Partly expired Specific authorization

An omnibus counterterrorism law passed six weeks after September 11. It widened surveillance and information-sharing authorities, expanded anti-money-laundering rules, and broadened terrorism offenses and immigration exclusions.





2002


Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq Resolution of 2002 Repealed Specific authorization

Authorized the President to use the armed forces to defend U.S. national security against the continuing threat posed by Iraq and to enforce relevant U.N. Security Council resolutions.





2002


Homeland Security Act of 2002 In force Framework statute

Created the Department of Homeland Security by merging 22 agencies, the largest federal reorganization since 1947.





2004


Intelligence Reform and Terrorism Prevention Act of 2004 In force Framework statute

Carried out the main recommendations of the 9/11 Commission. It separated leadership of the intelligence community from leadership of the CIA by creating the Director of National Intelligence.





2004


Millennium Challenge Act of 2003 In force Specific authorization

Created the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a small government corporation that gives large, multi-year grants to poor countries that pass a scorecard of governance, economic freedom, and social investment indicators.





2004


Support of Special Operations to Combat Terrorism (10 U.S.C. 127e) In force Targeted provision

Lets the Secretary of Defense fund foreign forces, irregular forces, groups, or individuals who support or facilitate ongoing U.S. special operations against terrorism.





2004


Hamdi v. Rumsfeld, 542 U.S. 507 Supreme Court

The 2001 AUMF authorizes detaining individuals who fought against the United States in Afghanistan as part of or supporting Taliban forces, including citizens, for the duration of the relevant hostilities.





2005


Detainee Treatment Act of 2005 In force Targeted provision

Known as the McCain Amendment, it prohibits cruel, inhuman, or degrading treatment of anyone in U.S. custody, wherever held, and ties Defense Department interrogations to the Army Field Manual.





2006


Military Commissions Act of 2006 In force Specific authorization

Passed after Hamdan v. Rumsfeld struck down the commissions created by presidential order, it gave statutory authority to try alien unlawful enemy combatants by military commission and defined the offenses and procedures.





2006


Hamdan v. Rumsfeld, 548 U.S. 557 Supreme Court

No. The commissions’ procedures violated the Uniform Code of Military Justice, which requires that commission rules match those of courts-martial as far as practicable, and Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions.





2008


FISA Amendments Act of 2008 Lapsed Specific authorization

Added Title VII to FISA. Section 702 lets the government target non-U.S. persons reasonably believed to be abroad, with compelled help from U.S. communications providers, under annual court-approved certifications instead of individual warrants.





2008


Boumediene v. Bush, 553 U.S. 723 Supreme Court

Yes, they have the privilege. Sec. 7 of the Military Commissions Act, which stripped federal courts of jurisdiction over their habeas petitions, operates as an unconstitutional suspension of the writ, and the review procedures of the Detainee Treatment Act are not an adequate substitute.





2010


Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project, 561 U.S. 1 Supreme Court

Yes, as applied to the plaintiffs’ proposed activities. The ban in 18 U.S.C. 2339B is not unconstitutionally vague and does not violate the First Amendment, given Congress’s and the executive’s judgment that any support frees resources for terrorism.

title: Timeline
text:
Sanctions, cyber, and great powers



2013


Clapper v. Amnesty International USA, 568 U.S. 398 Supreme Court

No. Their fear that their communications would be collected was too speculative to establish the concrete, imminent injury Article III requires, and their costs to avoid surveillance could not substitute for it.





2015


Cybersecurity Information Sharing Act of 2015 Partly expired Specific authorization

Enacted as Division N of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2016. It set up a voluntary system for companies and the federal government to share cyber threat indicators and defensive measures, with legal protection for companies that take part.





2015


Iran Nuclear Agreement Review Act of 2015 In force Specific authorization

Gives Congress a defined period to review any nuclear agreement with Iran before the President may waive or suspend statutory sanctions, and requires regular compliance certifications afterward.





2015


USA FREEDOM Act of 2015 Partly expired Specific authorization

The legislative response to the 2013 Snowden disclosures. It ended bulk collection of domestic telephone records and required that records requests be tied to a specific selection term.





2015


Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative (FY2016 NDAA, Sec. 1250) In force Targeted provision

The Defense Department’s authority to provide security assistance and intelligence support, including training, equipment, and logistics, to Ukraine’s military and other security forces.





2015


Zivotofsky v. Kerry, 576 U.S. 1 Supreme Court

No. The power to recognize foreign states and governments belongs to the President alone, and Sec. 214(d) of the Foreign Relations Authorization Act, Fiscal Year 2003, which required the listing, unconstitutionally infringed it.





2016


Global Magnitsky Human Rights Accountability Act In force Specific authorization

Authorizes visa bans and asset freezes against foreign individuals and entities responsible for serious human rights abuse or significant corruption anywhere in the world.





2016


Security Cooperation Reform (FY2017 NDAA, Title 10 Chapter 16) In force Framework statute

The FY2017 defense authorization gathered dozens of scattered Defense Department authorities for training, equipping, and advising foreign forces into a single chapter of Title 10, with common definitions, oversight, and evaluation rules.





2017


Annual Report on Civilian Casualties (FY2018 NDAA Sec. 1057) In force Targeted provision

Requires the Secretary of Defense to report to the congressional defense committees by May 1 each year on civilian casualties caused by U.S. military operations in the previous year.





2017


Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act In force Specific authorization

A three-part sanctions law aimed at Iran, Russia, and North Korea. Its Russia title wrote existing executive order sanctions into statute and gave Congress the power to block the President from easing them.





2017


Women, Peace, and Security Act of 2017 In force Specific authorization

Makes it U.S. policy to promote the meaningful participation of women in conflict prevention, peace negotiations, and post-conflict recovery, and requires a government-wide strategy to carry that out.





2018


Civilian Casualty Policy (FY2019 NDAA Sec. 936) In force Targeted provision

Directs the Under Secretary of Defense for Policy to designate a senior civilian official, at or above the Assistant Secretary level, to develop and oversee compliance with Defense Department policy on civilian casualties from U.S. military operations.





2018


Export Control Reform Act of 2018 In force Framework statute

The permanent statutory basis for Commerce Department controls on dual-use exports. It replaced the Export Administration Act of 1979, which had lapsed and been kept alive for years by emergency declarations.





2018


Foreign Investment Risk Review Modernization Act of 2018 In force Framework statute

Expanded the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States, which reviews foreign acquisitions for national security risk.





2018


Military Cyber Operations Authority (10 U.S.C. 394-395) In force Targeted provision

Affirms the Defense Department’s authority to conduct military operations in cyberspace, including clandestine ones and ones short of hostilities, and classifies clandestine military cyber activity as traditional military activity instead of covert action.





2019


Caesar Syria Civilian Protection Act of 2019 Repealed Specific authorization

Imposed secondary sanctions on foreign persons doing business with the Assad government’s military, energy, aviation, and reconstruction sectors.





2019


Elie Wiesel Genocide and Atrocities Prevention Act of 2018 In force Specific authorization

Declares that preventing genocide and other atrocities is a national interest of the United States and requires the executive branch to organize, train, and report accordingly.





2019


Ex Gratia Payments for Civilian Harm (FY2020 NDAA Sec. 1213) In force Targeted provision

Authorizes the Secretary of Defense to make ex gratia payments to foreign civilians for property damage, injury, or death incident to the use of force by U.S. forces, a coalition that includes the United States, or a military organization supporting either.





2019


Global Fragility Act of 2019 Partly expired Specific authorization

Enacted as Title V of Division J of the Further Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2020. It directs a ten-year, whole-of-government strategy to prevent violent conflict and stabilize fragile states, applied first in a small set of priority countries.





2022


Civilian Protection Center of Excellence (10 U.S.C. 184) In force Targeted provision

Requires the Secretary of Defense to operate a Civilian Protection Center of Excellence as the Department’s focal point for civilian casualties and other civilian harm from U.S. military operations.





2024


Reforming Intelligence and Securing America Act Lapsed Specific authorization

Reauthorized Section 702 for two years, the shortest extension to date, and made the most extensive changes to FISA since 2008, concentrated on how the FBI may search collected data for information about Americans.





2026


Coup Restriction (State-Foreign Operations Appropriations, Sec. 7008) In force Targeted provision

Bars the use of foreign assistance funds to finance assistance directly to the government of a country whose duly elected head of government is deposed by a military coup or decree, or by a coup or decree in which the military plays a decisive role.





2026


General Transfer Authority (Defense Appropriations Act, Sec. 8005) In force Targeted provision

The recurring section of the annual Defense appropriations act that lets the Secretary of Defense, with the approval of the Director of the Office of Management and Budget, move funds between accounts up to a cap set each year ($6 billion for fiscal 2026).





2026


Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump, 607 U.S. ___ Supreme Court

No. IEEPA does not authorize the President to impose tariffs. The Court affirmed the Federal Circuit’s judgment against the tariffs in the companion case and ordered the challenge brought in district court dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.

title: Glossary
text:
60-day clock

Under WPR Sec. 5(b), forces must be withdrawn within 60 days of a required report, plus 30 days for safe withdrawal, unless Congress authorizes the operation. From Unit 3: Deciding to use force.

Apportionment

The Office of Management and Budget’s division of an appropriation by time period or project, which agencies need before they may obligate funds. From Unit 4: The power of the purse.

Appropriation

Budget authority provided by law to incur obligations and make payments for specified purposes. No money may be drawn from the Treasury without one. From Unit 4: The power of the purse.

AUMF

An authorization for use of military force, a joint resolution that gives the President statutory authority to use force for a stated purpose. Modern AUMFs declare themselves the specific authorization the War Powers Resolution requires. From Unit 3: Deciding to use force.

Authorization

A law that establishes or continues an agency or program and may recommend funding levels, but does not itself provide money. From Unit 4: The power of the purse.

Blocking

Freezing property and interests in property within U.S. jurisdiction and prohibiting transactions in them, the core tool of IEEPA sanctions. From Unit 5: Emergency and economic powers.

Center of Excellence

The Civilian Protection Center of Excellence at 10 U.S.C. 184, the Department’s statutory focal point for civilian harm data, guidance, and lessons learned. From Unit 12: Civilian harm and the conduct of operations.

CFIUS

The Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States, which reviews foreign acquisitions and investments for national security risk. From Unit 11: Arms transfers, export controls, and investment screening.

Civilian harm mitigation and response

The Defense Department’s term, abbreviated CHMR, for preventing, mitigating, and responding to civilian casualties and other harm from military operations. From Unit 12: Civilian harm and the conduct of operations.

Combat exclusion

The Foreign Claims Act’s bar on claims arising from combat, which is why combat harm needs a separate ex gratia authority. From Unit 12: Civilian harm and the conduct of operations.

Combatant commander

The commander of a unified combatant command, who receives operational orders from the President through the Secretary of Defense. From Unit 8: Organizing and commanding the military.

Congressional notification

Advance notice to Congress of a proposed major arms sale, which opens a period in which Congress may pass a joint resolution of disapproval. From Unit 11: Arms transfers, export controls, and investment screening.

Continuing resolution

A joint resolution that funds agencies, usually at the prior year’s rate, when regular appropriations are not enacted. It generally bars new programs and production increases. From Unit 4: The power of the purse.

Covert action

Activity to influence conditions abroad where the U.S. role is intended not to be apparent or acknowledged. It requires a written presidential finding and notice to the intelligence committees. Defined at 50 U.S.C. 3093(e). From Unit 6: Intelligence and its oversight.

Declaration of war

A joint resolution or act under Article I declaring that a state of war exists. Congress has passed eleven, in five wars, the last in 1942. From Unit 1: Where the power comes from.

Deferral

A temporary withholding of funds, allowed under the Impoundment Control Act only for limited reasons and not past the end of the fiscal year. From Unit 4: The power of the purse.

Drawdown

Transfer of defense articles and services from existing U.S. stocks under Sec. 506 of the Foreign Assistance Act, replaced later with new appropriations. From Unit 11: Arms transfers, export controls, and investment screening.

Dual-use item

Goods, software, or technology with both civilian and military uses, controlled by the Commerce Department under ECRA. From Unit 11: Arms transfers, export controls, and investment screening.

Ex gratia payment

A voluntary payment to a harmed civilian or family that does not admit legal liability. Since 2019, Sec. 1213 of the FY2020 NDAA is the sole authority for such payments for harm from the use of force. From Unit 12: Civilian harm and the conduct of operations.

Federalization

Ordering Guard members into federal service under Title 10, which places them under the President and within Posse Comitatus limits unless an exception applies. From Unit 9: The military at home.

Finding

A written presidential determination that a covert action is necessary to support identifiable foreign policy objectives. From Unit 6: Intelligence and its oversight.

Foreign Military Sales

Government-to-government sales administered by the Defense Department, in contrast to direct commercial sales, which companies make under State Department export licenses. From Unit 11: Arms transfers, export controls, and investment screening.

Framework statute

A standing law that creates an institution or a general procedure that later laws and executive actions depend on. From Unit 2: Building the national security state, 1947 to 1958.

Hostilities

The War Powers Resolution’s trigger term, which it never defines. Most disputes over the resolution turn on whether an operation amounts to hostilities. From Unit 3: Deciding to use force.

Leahy vetting

Screening foreign security force units for credible information of gross violations of human rights before they receive U.S. assistance. From Unit 10: Foreign assistance, fragility, and partners.

National emergency

A presidential declaration under the National Emergencies Act that unlocks standby statutory powers. The President must specify which powers are being used, and emergencies lapse unless renewed each year. From Unit 5: Emergency and economic powers.

Obligation

A binding commitment, such as a contract or grant, that will require a payment. The Antideficiency Act bars obligations beyond, or in advance of, an appropriation. From Unit 4: The power of the purse.

Operational chain of command

The line of authority for military operations, which since 1958 runs from the President through the Secretary of Defense to the unified commands, not through the service departments. From Unit 2: Building the national security state, 1947 to 1958.

Positive law title

A U.S. Code title Congress has itself enacted, so the Code text is the law. Titles 10 and 32 are positive law; Titles 22 and 50 are not, so for them the Statutes at Large control. From Unit 1: Where the power comes from.

Reprogramming

Shifting funds within an account from one purpose to another, governed mainly by notification to the Appropriations Committees rather than by statute. From Unit 4: The power of the purse.

Rescission

A law cancelling budget authority before it is obligated. The President may propose one under the Impoundment Control Act. From Unit 4: The power of the purse.

Secondary sanctions

Penalties on foreign persons, not just U.S. persons, for dealing with a sanctioned country or sector. The Iran Sanctions Act pioneered them. From Unit 5: Emergency and economic powers.

Section 702

The FISA authority, added in 2008, to target non-U.S. persons reasonably believed to be abroad with compelled help from U.S. providers, under annual court-approved certifications instead of individual orders. From Unit 7: Surveillance law.

Security assistance

Programs under Title 22, run by the State Department, that provide defense articles, training, and services to foreign governments. From Unit 10: Foreign assistance, fragility, and partners.

Security assistance

Programs authorized mainly in Title 22 and funded in the State-foreign operations act, under State Department policy direction, such as FMF, IMET, and Peacekeeping Operations. From Unit 10: Foreign assistance, fragility, and partners.

Security cooperation

Defense Department activities with foreign security forces, such as training, equipping, and advising, mostly under Title 10 Chapter 16. From Unit 10: Foreign assistance, fragility, and partners.

Security cooperation

Defense Department activities with foreign forces under Title 10, consolidated in Chapter 16 in 2016, and overseen by the armed services committees. From Unit 10: Foreign assistance, fragility, and partners.

Statutes at Large

The official chronological publication of every law as enacted, cited by volume and page, for example 87 Stat. 555. From Unit 1: Where the power comes from.

Sunset

A date on which an authority expires unless Congress extends it. From Unit 7: Surveillance law.

Surrogate force

A foreign force supporting U.S. special operations toward U.S. objectives, funded under 10 U.S.C. 127e, as distinct from a partner force built up for its own missions. From Unit 8: Organizing and commanding the military.

Title 32 status

National Guard duty under the command of a state governor, often with federal funding. Posse Comitatus does not apply. From Unit 9: The military at home.

Traditional military activities

The exception that keeps military operations out of the covert action definition, and with it outside the finding process. From Unit 6: Intelligence and its oversight.

Traditional military activity

A military operation outside the covert action definition. Section 394 classifies clandestine military cyber activity this way. From Unit 8: Organizing and commanding the military.

Transfer

Moving budget authority from one appropriation account to another. Allowed only when a statute authorizes it, as Sec. 8005 does for the Defense Department. From Unit 4: The power of the purse.

U.S. person query

A search of lawfully collected data using a term associated with an American. RISAA’s changes concentrated on how the FBI may run them. From Unit 7: Surveillance law.

Unified combatant command

A command with forces from more than one service under a single commander, organized by region or function. From Unit 2: Building the national security state, 1947 to 1958.

title: Women, Peace, and Security Act of 2017
text:
In force Specific authorization Pub. L. 115-68 131 Stat. 1202 22 U.S.C. 2152j et seq.
Makes it U.S. policy to promote the meaningful participation of women in conflict prevention, peace negotiations, and post-conflict recovery, and requires a government-wide strategy to carry that out.

title: Women, Peace, and Security Act of 2017
text:
Key provisions

Required a national Women, Peace, and Security strategy, first issued in 2019, with agency implementation plans.
Training for diplomatic, development, and defense personnel.
Consultation with local women’s groups and reporting to Congress.

title: Women, Peace, and Security Act of 2017
text:
Why it matters
The United States was the first country to put the agenda of U.N. Security Council Resolution 1325 into a comprehensive statute. It is a companion to the Global Fragility Act in the prevention and stabilization field.

title: Uniform Code of Military Justice
text:
In force Framework statute Pub. L. 81-506 64 Stat. 107 10 U.S.C. 801-946a
The criminal code and court system of the U.S. armed forces. It replaced the separate Army and Navy disciplinary codes with one law for all services, defining military offenses, the types of courts-martial, the rights of the accused, and civilian appellate review.

title: Uniform Code of Military Justice
text:
Key provisions

Art. 2: who is subject to the code, including, since 2006, civilians accompanying forces in a contingency operation.
Art. 15: nonjudicial punishment by commanders for minor offenses.
Arts. 16-20: summary, special, and general courts-martial.
Arts. 77-134: the punitive articles, including Art. 92 on failure to obey a lawful order and Art. 134, the general article.
Arts. 141-146: the Court of Appeals for the Armed Forces, a civilian court.

title: Uniform Code of Military Justice
text:
Why it matters
It is the enforcement mechanism behind civilian control and the law of war inside the force: the duty to obey applies to lawful orders only. The Supreme Court measured the first Guantanamo commissions against it in Hamdan v. Rumsfeld, which led to the Military Commissions Act. Nearly all changes to it now arrive through the annual NDAA.

title: Uniform Code of Military Justice
text:
Current status
In force. Heavily revised by the Military Justice Act of 2016 (FY2017 defense authorization) and by the FY2022 defense authorization, which moved prosecution decisions for sexual assault, murder, and other covered offenses from commanders to independent special trial counsel, effective December 2023.
Last checked November 10, 2026.

title: Uniform Code of Military Justice
text:

Hamdan (2006). Held the commissions failed the UCMJ’s requirement that their procedures be uniform with courts-martial as far as practicable.

text:

Passed after the United States recognized the People’s Republic of China and ended formal relations with Taipei. It preserves unofficial ties, commits the United States to supply defensive arms, and states U.S. concern about any coercive resolution of Taiwan’s status.

title: Taiwan Relations Act
text:
Key provisions

Sec. 2: any non-peaceful effort to determine Taiwan’s future is a threat to peace and of grave concern to the United States.
Sec. 3: the United States will make available defensive arms, with the President and Congress determining what is needed.
Requires the United States to maintain the capacity to resist force or coercion against Taiwan.
Established the American Institute in Taiwan to conduct unofficial relations.

text:

Arms sales under it follow the Arms Export Control Act procedures, and recent financing and stockpile authorities came through the annual NDAA.

title: Title 50, U.S. Code: War and National Defense
text:
In force Code title overview 50 U.S.C. 1 et seq.
The title of the U.S. Code that collects the laws on war powers, emergency powers, intelligence, and economic defense. Unlike Title 10 it has no single design; it is a shelf holding statutes passed over two centuries.

title: Title 50, U.S. Code: War and National Defense
text:
Key provisions

Wartime authorities: the Alien Enemies Act (sec. 21) and the Trading with the Enemy Act (sec. 4301).
War and emergency powers: the War Powers Resolution (sec. 1541), the National Emergencies Act (sec. 1601), and the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (sec. 1701).
Intelligence: the National Security Act (sec. 3001), covert action and oversight (secs. 3091-3093), the CIA Act (sec. 3501), and FISA (sec. 1801).
Economic defense: the Defense Production Act (sec. 4501), foreign investment review (sec. 4565), and export controls (sec. 4801).
Manpower: the Military Selective Service Act (sec. 3801).

title: Title 50, U.S. Code: War and National Defense
text:
Why it matters
‘Title 50’ is shorthand for intelligence authority, above all covert action under a presidential finding, in contrast to military authority under Title 10. The shorthand understates the title: it also holds the main checks on presidential war and emergency power. The core of its intelligence chapters is the National Security Act.

title: Title 50, U.S. Code: War and National Defense
text:
Current status
In force. It is not positive law: it is an editorial compilation of separate statutes, so the underlying acts control. Many sections were renumbered in 2013 and the former appendix was folded into the main title in 2015.
Last checked November 10, 2026.

title: Title 22, U.S. Code: Foreign Relations and Intercourse
text:
In force Code title overview 22 U.S.C. 1 et seq.
The title of the U.S. Code for diplomacy and foreign assistance. It holds the State Department’s authorities, the Foreign Service, foreign aid, arms export controls, and most country-specific sanctions and policy statutes.

title: Title 22, U.S. Code: Foreign Relations and Intercourse
text:
Key provisions

Department of State organization and the Foreign Service, including chief of mission authority (sec. 3927).
Foreign assistance (sec. 2151 and following) and arms export control (sec. 2751 and following).
Participation in the United Nations (sec. 287) and registration of foreign agents (sec. 611).
Country and issue statutes, including the Taiwan Relations Act, Cuba and Russia sanctions laws, human rights sanctions, and the Global Fragility Act.

‘Title 22’ is shorthand for security assistance run by the State Department, in contrast to security cooperation run by the Defense Department under Title 10. The two foundations of that system are the Foreign Assistance Act and the Arms Export Control Act.

title: Symington and Glenn Amendments
text:
In force Targeted provision 22 U.S.C. 2799aa, 2799aa-1
Two nonproliferation amendments from 1976 and 1977 that cut off U.S. economic and military aid to countries that trade in nuclear enrichment or reprocessing technology outside international safeguards, or that test a nuclear device.

title: Symington and Glenn Amendments
text:
Key provisions

Symington (Sec. 101): aid cutoff for delivering or receiving unsafeguarded enrichment equipment or technology.
Glenn (Sec. 102): aid cutoff for reprocessing transfers, and mandatory sanctions when a non-nuclear-weapon state detonates a nuclear device.
Presidential waivers are available in narrow circumstances, and Congress has added country-specific waivers.

title: Symington and Glenn Amendments
text:
Why it matters
The Glenn sanctions were triggered against both India and Pakistan after their 1998 tests and then waived by legislation. They are the clearest case of aid conditionality used for nonproliferation, connecting the Foreign Assistance Act, the Arms Export Control Act, and the Atomic Energy Act.

title: Military Selective Service Act
text:
Partly expired Framework statute Pub. L. 80-759 62 Stat. 604 50 U.S.C. 3801 et seq.
The standing law of conscription. It requires men to register at 18 and maintains the Selective Service System so that a draft could be run if Congress and the President restored the power to induct.

title: Military Selective Service Act
text:
Key provisions

Registration of male citizens and most male residents aged 18 through 25.
Classification, deferment, and conscientious objector provisions.
Local boards and a lottery system for any future induction.
Induction authority lapsed in 1973; registration was suspended in 1975 and resumed in 1980.

title: Military Selective Service Act
text:

It is the legal basis of the all-volunteer force’s backstop. Any large war would test it before it tested the mobilization authorities. Proposals to automate registration or extend it to women usually move through the annual NDAA.

title: General Transfer Authority (Defense Appropriations Act, Sec. 8005)
text:
In force Targeted provision Pub. L. 119-75 140 Stat. 196
The recurring section of the annual Defense appropriations act that lets the Secretary of Defense, with the approval of the Director of the Office of Management and Budget, move funds between accounts up to a cap set each year ($6 billion for fiscal 2026). Transfers must be for higher-priority items based on unforeseen military requirements and may never fund an item Congress has denied.

title: General Transfer Authority (Defense Appropriations Act, Sec. 8005)
text:
Key provisions

A determination by the Secretary that the transfer is necessary in the national interest, and OMB approval.
An annual dollar cap; transfers among military personnel accounts do not count against it.
Only for higher-priority items based on unforeseen military requirements, and never where Congress denied the item.

title: General Transfer Authority (Defense Appropriations Act, Sec. 8005)
text:

The limits matter most in disputes: in 2019 the Defense Department used general transfer authority to move funds into counterdrug accounts for border barrier construction under Section 284 (counterdrug), alongside emergency construction under Section 2808 (construction), and litigation over whether the barrier was an item Congress had denied followed. The Antideficiency Act and the purpose statute (31 U.S.C. 1301(a)) are the background rules a transfer must still satisfy.

text:

text:

Sec. 394(a)-(b): authority to conduct military cyber activities to defend the United States and its allies, including outside areas of active hostilities.

text:

One of the standby powers unlocked by a national emergency. When a declared war or emergency requires use of the armed forces, the Secretary of Defense may build military construction projects that Congress never authorized, using unspent military construction funds.

title: Emergency Military Construction Authority (10 U.S.C. 2808)
text:

Trigger: a declaration of war, or a national emergency declared by the President that requires use of the armed forces.

Funding comes from military construction money already appropriated and not yet obligated.
Congress must be notified of each decision and its cost.

title: Emergency Military Construction Authority (10 U.S.C. 2808)

title: Reserve and National Guard Mobilization Authorities
text:
In force Framework statute Pub. L. 82-476 66 Stat. 481 10 U.S.C. 12301-12304b, 12406
The set of Title 10 provisions, descended from the Armed Forces Reserve Act of 1952 and earlier militia acts, that let the federal government order reserve forces and the National Guard to active duty. Each tier has its own trigger, size limit, and duration.

title: Reserve and National Guard Mobilization Authorities
text:
Key provisions

Sec. 12301(a): full mobilization in a war or national emergency declared by Congress, for the duration plus six months.
Sec. 12302: partial mobilization of up to 1,000,000 reservists for up to 24 months under a national emergency declared by the President.
Sec. 12304: presidential call-up of up to 200,000 reservists for up to 365 days without a declared emergency.
Secs. 12304a and 12304b: call-ups for disaster response and for preplanned missions supporting combatant commands.
Sec. 12406: the President may call the National Guard into federal service in case of invasion, rebellion, or inability to execute the laws with the regular forces.
By contrast, Guard members serving under Title 32 remain under state command while federally funded.

title: Reserve and National Guard Mobilization Authorities
text:
Why it matters
Which authority is used decides who commands the troops and what they may do: Guard members federalized under Title 10 fall under the Posse Comitatus Act, while those in state or Title 32 status do not. Section 12406 is an alternative route to the Insurrection Act, and Section 12302 depends on an emergency declared under the National Emergencies Act.

title: Reserve and National Guard Mobilization Authorities
text:
Current status
In force. On December 23, 2025 the Supreme Court, in Trump v. Illinois, left in place an order blocking a National Guard federalization under Section 12406(3), reasoning that ‘regular forces’ in that section likely means the regular military. The administration then ended its deployments under that section. The ruling came on an emergency application and litigation may continue. Check current status.
Last checked November 10, 2026.

title: USA PATRIOT Act
text:

An omnibus counterterrorism law passed six weeks after September 11. It widened surveillance and information-sharing authorities, expanded anti-money-laundering rules, and broadened terrorism offenses and immigration exclusions.

Sec. 215: orders for ‘any tangible things’ relevant to a terrorism or counterintelligence investigation.

Sec. 805: expanded the definition of material support for terrorism.

text:

title: National Emergencies Act
text:
In force Framework statute Pub. L. 94-412 90 Stat. 1255 50 U.S.C. 1601-1651
Ended the open-ended emergencies that had accumulated since the 1930s and set procedures for declaring, renewing, and terminating national emergencies. A declaration unlocks more than a hundred standby statutory powers, but the President must specify which ones are being used.

title: National Emergencies Act
text:
Key provisions

Title I: terminated powers exercised under emergencies in effect in 1976.
Sec. 201: the President declares an emergency by proclamation published in the Federal Register.
Sec. 202: emergencies lapse after one year unless renewed; Congress may terminate by joint resolution (changed from concurrent resolution in 1985) and is directed to consider termination every six months.
Sec. 301: the President must name the statutory authorities being invoked.
Title IV: accounting and reporting requirements.

title: National Emergencies Act
text:
Why it matters
It is the procedural gateway for IEEPA, so nearly every U.S. economic sanctions program rests on a declaration made under it. Because termination now requires a joint resolution that the President can veto, critics argue the check Congress intended in 1976 is much weaker in practice.

title: National Defense Act of 1916
text:
Superseded Framework statute Pub. L. 64-85 39 Stat. 166 10 U.S.C. 10101 et seq.
The first comprehensive statute organizing U.S. land forces. It defined the Army as the Regular Army, the National Guard, and a federal reserve, and it let the President draft the Guard into federal service for use overseas.

title: National Defense Act of 1916
text:
Key provisions

Defined the components of the Army and expanded its authorized strength.
Guard members took a dual oath to state and nation and could be drafted into federal service in war.
Created the Reserve Officers’ Training Corps and an organized reserve.
Gave the President authority to place obligatory orders with industry in war, an early precedent for defense production powers.

title: National Defense Act of 1916
text:
Why it matters
It set the three-component structure the Army still has. The 1933 amendments completed the design by making Guard members simultaneously members of a federal reserve component, which is what today’s mobilization authorities operate on. Its industrial mobilization section anticipates the Defense Production Act.

title: Millennium Challenge Act of 2003
text:
In force Specific authorization Pub. L. 108-199 118 Stat. 211 22 U.S.C. 7701 et seq.
Created the Millennium Challenge Corporation, a small government corporation that gives large, multi-year grants to poor countries that pass a scorecard of governance, economic freedom, and social investment indicators. It was enacted as Title VI of Division D of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2004.

title: Millennium Challenge Act of 2003

Key provisions

Eligibility determined by a board using published third-party indicators.
Compacts of up to five years negotiated with and implemented by the partner country.
Threshold programs for countries that fall just short of eligibility.

It was designed as an alternative to the model in the Foreign Assistance Act: selective, country-led, and insulated from short-term foreign policy uses of aid. It is the standard example in debates about aid selectivity.

title: Military Commissions Act of 2006
text:
In force Specific authorization Pub. L. 109-366 120 Stat. 2600 10 U.S.C. 948a-950t
Passed after Hamdan v. Rumsfeld struck down the commissions created by presidential order, it gave statutory authority to try alien unlawful enemy combatants by military commission and defined the offenses and procedures.

title: Military Commissions Act of 2006
text:
Key provisions

Added chapter 47A to Title 10: jurisdiction, procedures, and triable offenses for military commissions.
Sec. 7: removed habeas jurisdiction over detained alien enemy combatants, held unconstitutional in Boumediene v. Bush (2008).
Amended the War Crimes Act to narrow which Common Article 3 violations are federal crimes.
2009 revision: tighter rules on coerced statements and hearsay, and better access to counsel and evidence.

title: Military Commissions Act of 2006

title: Lend-Lease Act
text:
Superseded Specific authorization Pub. L. 77-11 55 Stat. 31
Authorized the President to sell, transfer, lend, or lease defense articles to any country whose defense he judged vital to the defense of the United States. It ended the cash-and-carry limits of the 1930s neutrality laws nine months before Pearl Harbor.

title: Lend-Lease Act
text:
Key provisions

Transfer of defense articles and information to countries whose defense the President deemed vital to the United States.
Terms of repayment left to the President, ‘in kind or property, or any other direct or indirect benefit’.
Reporting to Congress and a provision for termination by concurrent resolution.

title: Lend-Lease Act
text:
Why it matters
It is the origin of large-scale U.S. arms transfers as an instrument of policy short of war. Its postwar successors were the Mutual Security Act and then the framework split between the Foreign Assistance Act and the Arms Export Control Act.

title: Lend-Lease Act

title: Intelligence Oversight Act of 1980
text:

Enacted as part of the FY1981 intelligence authorization, it added the oversight title to the National Security Act. The executive branch must keep the two intelligence committees fully and currently informed of intelligence activities, including significant anticipated ones.

title: Intelligence Oversight Act of 1980
text:
Key provisions

50 U.S.C. 3091: general duty to keep the intelligence committees fully and currently informed.
50 U.S.C. 3093: covert action requires a written presidential finding, may not be retroactive, and must be reported to the committees.
Limited notification in extraordinary circumstances to eight congressional leaders, the ‘Gang of Eight’.

title: Intelligence Oversight Act of 1980
text:
Why it matters
This is the standing legal basis for congressional intelligence oversight. It cut the number of committees notified under the Hughes-Ryan Amendment from eight to two, and it is the source of the statutory definition of covert action that separates CIA activity from traditional military activity.

title: International Military Education and Training (Foreign Assistance Act, Sec. 541)
text:
In force Targeted provision Pub. L. 94-329 90 Stat. 732 22 U.S.C. 2347 and following
Grant-funded professional military education and training, in the United States and abroad, for foreign military personnel and related civilians. Added to the Foreign Assistance Act in 1976, it aims at professionalization, civilian control of the military, and respect for human rights as well as technical skill, and it builds long-term ties with future military leaders.

title: International Military Education and Training (Foreign Assistance Act, Sec. 541)
text:
Key provisions

Sec. 541(a): the President may furnish military education and training to military and related civilian personnel of foreign countries, on a reimbursable basis whenever feasible.
Civilians, including officials outside defense ministries, legislators, and nongovernmental participants, qualify when training serves defense resource management, civilian control of the military, counternarcotics cooperation, or military justice and human rights (often called Expanded IMET).
Training may be at U.S. military schools other than the service academies, in special courses, or through orientation visits.
Sec. 541(b): countries that buy training with FMF are charged a rate comparable to grant IMET.
Recipient units and individuals are subject to Leahy Laws vetting.

title: International Military Education and Training (Foreign Assistance Act, Sec. 541)
text:
Why it matters
IMET is small in dollars but large in reach: it puts foreign officers through U.S. staff colleges and war colleges, and its graduates often rise to senior command. It is also among the first programs suspended when a partner’s military seizes power under the coup restriction and among the first restored, which makes it a frequent subject of country-specific conditions.

title: International Military Education and Training (Foreign Assistance Act, Sec. 541)
text:

Last checked November 24, 2026.

Committees. Authorizing, House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations; appropriations, the House and Senate subcommittees for State and foreign operations.

title: Foreign Military Sales (Arms Export Control Act, Secs. 21-22)
text:
In force Targeted provision Pub. L. 90-629 82 Stat. 1323 22 U.S.C. 2761-2762
The government-to-government channel for selling U.S. defense articles, services, and training. The Defense Department sells from its own stocks (Sec. 21) or buys from industry on the purchaser’s behalf (Sec. 22), and the purchaser pays the full cost, normally in advance, so the articles themselves need no appropriation.

title: Foreign Military Sales (Arms Export Control Act, Secs. 21-22)
text:
Key provisions

Sec. 21(a): sales from Defense Department stocks at actual value or replacement cost; services at full cost.
Sec. 21(c): U.S. personnel performing services under a sale may not perform duties of a combatant nature, with reporting to Congress if hostilities endanger them.
Sec. 21(e): purchasers pay charges that recover the administrative costs of the program.
Sec. 22(a): procurement for a purchaser on its dependable undertaking to pay the full contract cost.
Major sales above dollar thresholds require notice to Congress under Sec. 36(b) of the Arms Export Control Act, and a joint resolution can block them.

title: Foreign Military Sales (Arms Export Control Act, Secs. 21-22)
text:
Why it matters
FMS is how most major U.S. weapons reach foreign governments, and grant money from Foreign Military Financing is usually spent through it. Because the State Department approves each case and the Defense Department executes it, oversight runs through the Arms Export Control Act notification process rather than through appropriations.

title: Foreign Military Sales (Arms Export Control Act, Secs. 21-22)
text:
Current status

Last checked November 24, 2026.

title: Foreign Military Sales (Arms Export Control Act, Secs. 21-22)
text:

title: FISA Amendments Act of 2008
text:
Lapsed Specific authorization Pub. L. 110-261 122 Stat. 2436 50 U.S.C. 1881-1881g
Added Title VII to FISA. Section 702 lets the government target non-U.S. persons reasonably believed to be abroad, with compelled help from U.S. communications providers, under annual court-approved certifications instead of individual warrants.

title: FISA Amendments Act of 2008
text:
Key provisions

Sec. 702: programmatic collection approved by the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court through annual certifications, with targeting, minimization, and querying procedures.
Secs. 703-704: individualized court orders required to target U.S. persons abroad.
Title II: retroactive liability protection for telecommunications companies that assisted the post-2001 warrantless program.

title: FISA Amendments Act of 2008
text:
Why it matters
It replaced the temporary Protect America Act of 2007 and gave a statutory footing to collection that began under claims of authority from the 2001 AUMF. The persistent dispute is over ‘backdoor searches’: queries of 702 data using Americans’ identifiers without a warrant. That dispute shaped RISAA and the 2026 lapse.

title: FISA Amendments Act of 2008
text:
Current status
Title VII, including Section 702, lapsed in mid-June 2026 for the first time since 2008, after two short extensions in April 2026 and a failed Senate vote. Collection can continue under existing court certifications, reported to run to March 2027. No reauthorization had been enacted as of this wiki’s last review (November 10, 2026). Check current status before relying on this page.

title: Ex Gratia Payments for Civilian Harm (FY2020 NDAA Sec. 1213)
text:
In force Targeted provision Pub. L. 116-92 133 Stat. 1629 10 U.S.C. 2731 note
Authorizes the Secretary of Defense to make ex gratia payments to foreign civilians for property damage, injury, or death incident to the use of force by U.S. forces, a coalition that includes the United States, or a military organization supporting either. A payment is not an admission of legal liability, and the section is the sole authority for such payments.

title: Ex Gratia Payments for Civilian Harm (FY2020 NDAA Sec. 1213)
text:
Key provisions

Sec. 1213(a): up to $3,000,000 a year from Defense-wide operation and maintenance funds, through December 31, 2033.
Sec. 1213(b): conditions, including that the harm is not compensable under the Foreign Claims Act, was not caused by an enemy, was caused by U.S., coalition, or supporting forces, and befell a recipient with no part in the hostile act.
Sec. 1213(c): a payment is not an admission or acknowledgment of any legal obligation to compensate.
Sec. 1213(d): procedures, added in 2021, to receive and respond to civilian harm allegations through formal acknowledgment, a nonmonetary expression of condolence, or a payment.
Sec. 1213(h): quarterly reports to the congressional defense committees on payments made, refused, denied, or pending.
Sec. 1213(i): the sole authority for ex gratia payments for harm incident to the use of force.

title: Ex Gratia Payments for Civilian Harm (FY2020 NDAA Sec. 1213)
text:

It fills the combat gap left by the Foreign Claims Act. Earlier ex gratia programs ran through provisions in annual appropriations acts; Sec. 1213(i) now makes this the sole authority. Its 2021 amendments tied the payment and acknowledgment process to the civilian casualty policy.

text:

title: Department of Defense Reorganization Act of 1958
text:
In force Framework statute Pub. L. 85-599 72 Stat. 514 10 U.S.C. 113, 162, 164
President Eisenhower’s reorganization. It took the military departments out of the operational chain of command, so that orders run from the President and the Secretary of Defense to unified commands, and it confirmed the Secretary’s authority, direction, and control over the whole department.

title: Department of Defense Reorganization Act of 1958
text:
Key provisions

Operational command runs from the President to the Secretary of Defense to unified and specified commands.
The military departments are limited to organizing, training, and equipping forces.
Strengthened the Secretary’s power to reorganize and to assign functions, and created a director of defense research and engineering.
Current law: 10 U.S.C. 113(b) gives the Secretary authority, direction, and control; Sec. 162 assigns forces to combatant commands; Sec. 164 defines combatant command authority.

title: Department of Defense Reorganization Act of 1958
text:

It is the missing step between the National Security Act and the Goldwater-Nichols Act. The 1986 act was needed largely because the services kept, in practice, much of the influence this act removed on paper. Sections 113, 162, and 164 are the ‘Title 10 chain of command’ referred to in debates about who may direct military operations.

title: Department of Defense Reorganization Act of 1958

title: Department of Defense Appropriations Act (annual series)
text:
In force Specific authorization Pub. L. 119-75 140 Stat. 174
The annual law that provides the Defense Department’s money. The NDAA sets policy and authorizes amounts; this act makes funds available to obligate, account by account, and attaches general provisions that limit how they may be used. The series began with the National Military Establishment Appropriation Act, 1950 (Pub. L. 81-434), the first single appropriation for the newly unified military.

title: Department of Defense Appropriations Act (annual series)
text:
Key provisions

Titles I-VII: military personnel; operation and maintenance; procurement; research, development, test and evaluation; revolving funds; other programs; related agencies.
Title VIII general provisions recur each year, on transfers, reprogramming, multiyear contracts, and limits on the use of funds.
Sec. 8005 (FY2026): general transfer authority of up to $6 billion between accounts, only for higher-priority, unforeseen military requirements and never for an item Congress has denied.
Military construction and family housing are funded in a separate act, the Military Construction, Veterans Affairs, and Related Agencies appropriations.

title: Department of Defense Appropriations Act (annual series)
text:
Why it matters
Authorization without appropriation spends nothing, so this act is where Congress’s control of the military is most concrete. Funding prohibitions in it have ended or limited operations, as the Case-Church Amendment and the Boland Amendments did, and its transfer authority (Sec. 8005 transfers) sets how far the Department can move money Congress assigned elsewhere. When the act is late, the Department runs on continuing resolutions that generally bar new programs and production increases. Members and staff who want to change defense policy without a new authorization usually look here first.

title: Civilian Protection Center of Excellence (10 U.S.C. 184)
text:
In force Targeted provision Pub. L. 117-263 136 Stat. 2799 10 U.S.C. 184
Requires the Secretary of Defense to operate a Civilian Protection Center of Excellence as the Department’s focal point for civilian casualties and other civilian harm from U.S. military operations. The statute assigns it specific functions, from standardized harm reporting to a repository of casualty data and lessons learned.

title: Civilian Protection Center of Excellence (10 U.S.C. 184)
text:
Key provisions

10 U.S.C. 184(a): the center is the focal point for civilian harm matters and institutionalizes practices for preventing, mitigating, and responding to harm.
10 U.S.C. 184(b)(1), (5): standardized civilian harm reporting and data processes, and a repository of civilian casualty and harm information.
10 U.S.C. 184(b)(6): lessons learned from assessments and investigations, built into policy, doctrine, training, and tactics.
10 U.S.C. 184(b)(7)-(8): coordination with the combatant commands and the State Department, and engagement with nongovernmental organizations.
10 U.S.C. 184(c): a public annual report on the center’s activities.

title: Civilian Protection Center of Excellence (10 U.S.C. 184)

Enacted as Sec. 1082 of the FY2023 defense authorization, it wrote into permanent law an institution proposed in the Protection of Civilians in Military Operations Act (H.R. 7625, 117th Congress). Because it sits in Title 10, the Department cannot abolish it administratively, which made the statute the center of the 2025 and 2026 dispute over civilian harm staffing. It carries out the civilian casualty policy.

Requires the Secretary of Defense to report to the congressional defense committees by May 1 each year on civilian casualties caused by U.S. military operations in the previous year. The unclassified report must be made public when it is submitted unless the Secretary certifies in writing that publication would threaten U.S. national security interests.

title: Annual Report on Civilian Casualties (FY2018 NDAA Sec. 1057)
text:
Key provisions

Sec. 1057(a): annual report, due May 1, on civilian casualties from U.S. military operations in the preceding year.
Sec. 1057(b)(1)-(2): each operation, strike, raid, or incident with confirmed or reasonably suspected civilian casualties, with its date, location, whether it was inside a declared theater of active armed conflict, the authority used, and casualty estimates.
Sec. 1057(b)(6): the general reasons for discrepancies between U.S. assessments and nongovernmental reporting.
Sec. 1057(c): the Department must take into account credible all-source reporting, including public and nongovernmental reports.
Sec. 1057(d): unclassified form, published when submitted, with an optional classified annex.

title: Annual Report on Civilian Casualties (FY2018 NDAA Sec. 1057)
text:
Why it matters
It is the main public accounting of civilian harm from U.S. operations and the document most often cited when the Department and outside monitors dispute casualty counts. Congress has widened it in most later defense authorizations. It works alongside the civilian casualty policy, which governs how allegations are assessed and investigated.

title: Annual Report on Civilian Casualties (FY2018 NDAA Sec. 1057)

title: Central Intelligence Agency Act of 1949
text:
In force Framework statute Pub. L. 81-110 63 Stat. 208 50 U.S.C. 3501-3523
Gave the CIA the administrative tools to operate in secret: authority to spend money without the usual accounting rules, to withhold information about its staff and structure, and to procure and transfer funds confidentially.

title: Central Intelligence Agency Act of 1949
text:

Sec. 5: transfer and receipt of funds from other agencies without regard to normal appropriations limits.
Sec. 6: exemption from laws requiring disclosure of the agency’s organization, functions, names, titles, salaries, or staff numbers.

title: Case-Church Amendment
text:
Lapsed Targeted provision Pub. L. 93-50 87 Stat. 129
The funding cutoff that ended U.S. combat in Indochina. Section 307 of the Second Supplemental Appropriations Act, 1973 barred the use of its funds to support, directly or indirectly, combat by U.S. forces in or over Cambodia, Laos, North Vietnam, and South Vietnam or off their shores, and barred any previously appropriated funds for that purpose after August 15, 1973.

title: Case-Church Amendment
text:
Key provisions

Sec. 307: no funds under the act for direct or indirect support of U.S. combat activities in or over Cambodia, Laos, North Vietnam, and South Vietnam, or off their shores.
After August 15, 1973, the same bar applied to funds appropriated under any other act.
Named for Senators Clifford Case and Frank Church.

title: Case-Church Amendment
text:
Why it matters
The clearest example of Congress ending a military operation with the purse rather than a vote on the war itself. U.S. bombing in Cambodia stopped on the August 15 deadline. It passed four months before the War Powers Resolution and two years after Congress repealed the Gulf of Tonkin Resolution, and it remains the model for later proposals to cut off funds for a specific operation.

title: Case-Church Amendment
text:
Current status
Its funding prohibition applied to the appropriations it covered and is no longer operative. Of historical and precedential interest.
Last checked November 24, 2026.
