title: Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act
text:
In force Specific authorization Pub. L. 115-44 131 Stat. 886 22 U.S.C. 9401 et seq.
A three-part sanctions law aimed at Iran, Russia, and North Korea. Its Russia title wrote existing executive order sanctions into statute and gave Congress the power to block the President from easing them.

title: Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act
text:
Key provisions

Title I: sanctions on Iran’s ballistic missile program and the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps.
Sec. 216: congressional review, with a possible resolution of disapproval, before Russia sanctions are eased.
Sec. 231: sanctions on anyone making a significant transaction with Russia’s defense or intelligence sectors.
Title III: North Korea sanctions on shipping, labor, and finance.

title: Countering America’s Adversaries Through Sanctions Act
text:
Why it matters
Section 231 turned sanctions into an arms-transfer policy tool. It was applied to Turkey’s defense procurement agency over the S-400 purchase and has shaped U.S. dealings with India, so it interacts with the Arms Export Control Act. Like the Global Magnitsky Act it is carried out through IEEPA.

title: Authorization for Use of Military Force (2001)
text:
In force Specific authorization Pub. L. 107-40 115 Stat. 224 50 U.S.C. 1541 note
Enacted a week after the September 11 attacks, this joint resolution authorizes the President to use all necessary and appropriate force against the nations, organizations, or persons that planned, authorized, committed, or aided the attacks, or that harbored those who did.

title: Authorization for Use of Military Force (2001)
text:
Key provisions

Sec. 2(a): the operative grant of authority, tied to responsibility for the September 11 attacks.
Sec. 2(b): declares the resolution to be specific statutory authorization under the War Powers Resolution.
Contains no geographic limit, no named enemy, and no expiration date.

title: Authorization for Use of Military Force (2001)
text:
Why it matters
Successive administrations have read it to cover al-Qaeda, the Taliban, and ‘associated forces’, and later the Islamic State, in countries far from Afghanistan. It also underpins wartime detention at Guantanamo, which links it to the Detainee Treatment Act and the Military Commissions Act. Proposals to repeal or replace it recur in most Congresses.

title: Authorization for Use of Military Force (2001)
text:
Current status
In force with no sunset. It survived the December 2025 repeal of the two Iraq authorizations and remains the main statutory basis for counterterrorism operations.
Last checked November 10, 2026.

title: Authorization for Use of Military Force (2001)

title: Alien Enemies Act of 1798
text:
In force Framework statute 1 Stat. 577 50 U.S.C. 21-24
The only one of the Alien and Sedition Acts still in force. During a declared war, or an invasion or predatory incursion by a foreign nation or government, the President may detain, restrict, and remove nationals of the hostile country.

title: Alien Enemies Act of 1798
text:
Key provisions

Trigger: a declared war, or an invasion or predatory incursion perpetrated, attempted, or threatened by a foreign nation or government.
Applies to natives, citizens, denizens, or subjects of the hostile nation aged fourteen and older who are not naturalized.
The President sets the terms by proclamation; courts may hear whether a person falls within the act.

title: Alien Enemies Act of 1798
text:
Why it matters
Used in the War of 1812 and both world wars, it is the oldest wartime authority in Title 50 and the counterpart for persons of what the Trading with the Enemy Act does for property. The dispute since 2025 is whether its triggers can be met without one of the Declarations of War and by a non-state group.

title: Alien Enemies Act of 1798
text:
Current status
In force. A March 2025 proclamation invoked it against alleged members of a Venezuelan gang, its first use outside a declared war. The Supreme Court required notice and a chance to seek habeas review and later blocked removals of the plaintiffs. A Fifth Circuit panel found the invocation unlawful in September 2025; that opinion was vacated, and in August 2026 the full court dismissed the case as moot without ruling on the question. Check current status.
Last checked November 10, 2026.

title: Arms Export Control Act
text:
In force Framework statute Pub. L. 94-329 90 Stat. 729 22 U.S.C. 2751 et seq.
Governs U.S. arms exports. It sets the purposes for which American weapons may be sold, requires licenses for commercial sales, and gives Congress advance notice of major sales and a procedure to block them.

title: Arms Export Control Act
text:
Key provisions

Secs. 3 and 4: recipients may use U.S. arms only for self-defense, internal security, and similar purposes, and may not retransfer them without consent.
Sec. 36(b) and (c): notification to Congress of government and commercial sales above dollar thresholds, subject to a joint resolution of disapproval.
Sec. 36 emergency provision: the President may bypass the review period by declaring an emergency.
Sec. 38: licensing of commercial exports under the U.S. Munitions List and the International Traffic in Arms Regulations.
Sec. 40A: end-use monitoring.

title: Arms Export Control Act
text:
Why it matters
Congress has never blocked a sale through a resolution of disapproval that survived a veto, so its influence runs through informal holds and conditions. The act pairs with the Foreign Assistance Act on the assistance side, with the Export Control Reform Act for dual-use goods, and is limited by the Leahy Laws and the Symington-Glenn Amendments.

title: Arms Export Control Act
text:

Official means a federal government domain (.gov or .mil): GovInfo, Congress.gov, the U.S. Code, the House Clerk, and members’ official House sites. Everything else, such as news reports, think tank analysis, and trackers, is marked secondary and is used for current status or for facts no official page states. title: Sources
text:
How statute links are built
Each statute page links to two official texts, both on GovInfo, the Government Publishing Office’s authenticated repository:

Enacted text. The public law as passed, for the 104th Congress (1995) onward, or otherwise the law as printed in the Statutes at Large. GovInfo holds every volume of the Statutes at Large back to 1789, so even the Militia Acts of 1792 link to their original printing.
Current U.S. Code. The section as codified today, from GovInfo’s edition of the Code. Where a law sits in a statutory note, the link opens the section that carries the note.

Links are built from each statute’s citation by the patterns in the GovInfo link service documentation, so they are only as accurate as the citation. Two kinds of entry have no citation of their own: the Constitution page links to Constitution Annotated on Congress.gov, and composite pages such as the annual defense authorization link to specific enacted laws listed in their sources.

title: Zivotofsky v. Kerry
text:
Supreme Court 576 U.S. 1 Decided June 8, 2015 6 to 3
Holding. No. The power to recognize foreign states and governments belongs to the President alone, and Sec. 214(d) of the Foreign Relations Authorization Act, Fiscal Year 2003, which required the listing, unconstitutionally infringed it.
Question. Whether Congress could require the State Department, on request, to list “Israel” as the place of birth in the passports of U.S. citizens born in Jerusalem, contrary to the executive’s policy of not recognizing any state’s sovereignty over the city.
Background reading: Wikipedia article on Zivotofsky v. Kerry (secondary source).

title: Zivotofsky v. Kerry
text:
Why it matters
The Court upheld the President’s refusal to follow a foreign affairs statute, finding the power exclusive even in the third, “lowest ebb” category of Jackson’s framework; the Chief Justice’s dissent called it the first time the Court had accepted “a President’s direct defiance of an Act of Congress in the field of foreign affairs.” At the same time it declined to treat Curtiss-Wright’s “sole organ” language as making the President’s foreign affairs power exclusive in general, and it stressed Congress’s many powers in the field.

title: Zivotofsky v. Kerry
text:
Status
Good law.

title: Zivotofsky v. Kerry
text:
Statutes at issue

Constitution (war powers). Held the recognition power is exclusively the President’s, and rejected a general reading of Curtiss-Wright’s ‘sole organ’ language.

Studied in Unit 1: Where the power comes from.

title: Train v. City of New York
text:
Supreme Court 420 U.S. 35 Decided February 18, 1975 9 to 0
Holding. No. The statute required the Administrator to allot the full sums authorized; he had no discretion to withhold them. The Court decided the case on the statute alone and did not reach the constitutional question.
Question. Whether the Administrator of the Environmental Protection Agency, at President Nixon’s direction, could allot to the states less than the full amounts authorized for sewage treatment grants under the Federal Water Pollution Control Act Amendments of 1972.
Background reading: Wikipedia article on Train v. New York (secondary source).

title: Train v. City of New York
text:
Why it matters
The Supreme Court’s only decision on the Nixon impoundments. It shows how courts approach a refusal to spend: as a question of what the spending statute requires, not of inherent presidential power. That framing carries into disputes under the Impoundment Control Act, which gives the Comptroller General a statutory right to sue.

title: Train v. City of New York
text:
How Congress responded
Congress had already acted: the Impoundment Control Act was enacted in July 1974, while the case was pending.

title: Hamdi v. Rumsfeld
text:
Supreme Court 542 U.S. 507 Decided June 28, 2004 Plurality opinion; judgment 6 to 3
Holding. The 2001 AUMF authorizes detaining individuals who fought against the United States in Afghanistan as part of or supporting Taliban forces, including citizens, for the duration of the relevant hostilities. A citizen detainee must nonetheless receive notice of the factual basis for his classification and a fair opportunity to rebut it before a neutral decisionmaker.
Question. Whether the government could hold a U.S. citizen captured in Afghanistan as an enemy combatant, and what process he was due to contest that designation.
Background reading: Wikipedia article on Hamdi (secondary source).

title: Hamdi v. Rumsfeld
text:
Why it matters
The plurality read the 2001 AUMF’s “necessary and appropriate force” to include detention as a fundamental incident of war, a reading later codified in the FY2012 NDAA. Its statement that “a state of war is not a blank check for the President” is a standard reference in debates over wartime authority.

The Court struck down a provision Congress had enacted in response to its own earlier ruling in Hamdan, and, as Justice Scalia’s dissent put it, for the first time extended constitutional habeas to noncitizens held by the military abroad. It opened years of habeas litigation in federal court in Washington, which, rather than new legislation, defined the detention standard in practice.

title: About this wiki
text:
Scope
The wiki covers the federal statutes that most shape U.S. national security policy, the appropriations that fund them, and the Supreme Court decisions that define them, in these areas:

War powers and use of force
Appropriations and the power of the purse
Intelligence and surveillance
Foreign aid, fragility, and sanctions
Defense organization and arms transfers
Civilian harm and protection
Related foreign policy legislation

A further group, constitutional and code foundations, holds what the rest is built on: the Constitution’s war and foreign affairs clauses, the founding-era statutes, the laws that created the National Guard, and overview pages for Titles 10, 22, 32, and 50 of the U.S. Code.
Some entries are single provisions rather than whole acts, where the provision matters more than the act that carried it: 10 U.S.C. 127e, the civilian harm sections of recent defense authorizations, recurring appropriations provisions such as the coup restriction, and the sections that authorize programs such as Foreign Military Financing and IMET. Program entries add a section on funding and administration: the account, the appropriations act, the agency that runs it, and the committees of jurisdiction. They do not track dollar amounts.
Court cases have their own pages. Treaties, executive orders, Defense Department instructions, and regulations appear where they explain a statute but do not have pages. The Who’s who page covers the committees, agencies, and courts that recur across the wiki.

title: About this wiki
text:
Reading a statute page
Each page has the same parts: a citation bar whose citations link to the official text; the law’s status and layer; a summary that leads with what the law does; buttons to the enacted text and the current code; key provisions; why the law matters; its current status and the date it was last checked; for programs, funding and administration; the court cases that interpreted it; where it sits (layer, what it builds on, code title, era, study units, who is involved); its connections to other entries; and sources.
Links to repealed and superseded statutes are marked with a dagger (†).

title: About this wiki
text:
Relationship types
Connections are directional and use a fixed vocabulary.







Relationship
Meaning




amends
The first statute changed the text of the second.


repeals
The first statute repealed the second, in whole or in part.


succeeds
The first statute took over the role of the second.


relies on
The first statute operates through authority or machinery in the second.


constrains
The first statute limits how the second may be used.


enacted in
The first statute was passed as part of the second, usually a defense authorization.


part of
The first entry is a section within the second act.


funded through
The first entry’s program is paid for by the second, an appropriations act.


related to
A thematic or historical link without a direct legal dependency.


ruled on
A court case decided a question about the statute.



Amends, relies on, enacted in, succeeds, part of, and funded through count as dependencies: they make up a statute’s “builds on” and “built upon by” lists.

title: About this wiki
text:
Layers







Layer
Meaning




Constitution
The grants and limits every statute draws on.


Framework statute
A standing law that creates an institution or a general procedure other laws plug into.


Specific authorization
A law aimed at a particular conflict, country, program, or problem, usually working through a framework statute. The annual appropriations series are listed here.


Targeted provision
A single section that grants a narrow authority, imposes a condition, or requires a report. Program authorities are listed here.


U.S. Code title
The subject shelf where enacted law is filed.



Layer assignments are editorial judgments, not legal categories.

title: About this wiki
text:
Status labels







Status
Meaning




In force
The statute is current law. It may have been amended.


Partly expired
Core provisions are current, but significant authorities have lapsed or depend on short extensions.


Lapsed
The central authority expired, or a funding limit applied only to past appropriations.


Repealed
Congress repealed the statute.


Superseded
A later statute replaced it.

title: About this wiki
text:
Accuracy and limits
The summaries were drafted with Claude, an AI model. Each statute page shows when it was last checked. The entries added on November 24, 2026 were checked against the GovInfo text of the U.S. Code, the Statutes at Large, the enacted fiscal year 2026 appropriations act (Pub. L. 119-75), and the official opinions in the United States Reports on GovInfo or on the Supreme Court’s site. The civilian harm entries were checked against GovInfo in the November 10 review. Other citations and section numbers were written from reference knowledge and have not each been checked against the primary text.
Treat the wiki as a map for finding and relating the law. Before citing a provision in a memo, letter, or bill, confirm it in the official text linked on each page. Statutes with sunset clauses or disputed implementation change fastest; their status notes end with “Check current status.”
This is a reference tool and not legal advice.

title: About this wiki
text:
Adding or changing content
All content lives in data/. The pages in statutes/, cases/, and study/units/ are generated and should not be edited by hand.

Add or edit a statute in one of the files in data/statutes/, a case in data/cases.yml, or a Who’s who entry in data/institutions.yml. Copy an existing entry to get the fields right.
Add rows to data/edges.csv for a statute’s connections, using the relationship types above. A program with a funding field needs a matching “funded through” row.
Add the entry to a unit in data/study/units.yml.
Run Rscript R/deploy.R check. The build stops with a message if an ID, domain, layer, status, or relationship is not recognized, and the check then tests every internal link.

title: Immigration and Naturalization Service v. Chadha
text:
Supreme Court 462 U.S. 919 Decided June 23, 1983 7 to 2
Holding. No. Action with the effect of law must pass both houses and be presented to the President. One-house and two-house legislative vetoes are unconstitutional.
Question. Whether one house of Congress could, by resolution, override an executive decision to suspend an individual’s deportation, as the immigration statute then allowed.
Background reading: Wikipedia article on INS v. Chadha (secondary source).

title: Immigration and Naturalization Service v. Chadha
text:
Why it matters
Chadha invalidated the legislative veto device built into many national security statutes of the 1970s. It cast doubt on the War Powers Resolution provision letting Congress order a withdrawal by concurrent resolution and on the original concurrent-resolution procedures of the National Emergencies Act and the Arms Export Control Act, and it is why most congressional checks in this wiki now take the form of joint resolutions, which the President can veto.

title: Immigration and Naturalization Service v. Chadha
text:
How Congress responded
Congress replaced the vetoes with joint resolutions: expedited joint resolution procedures for the War Powers Resolution (1983), joint resolutions to terminate national emergencies (1985), and joint resolutions of disapproval for arms sales (1986).

title: Immigration and Naturalization Service v. Chadha
text:
Status
Good law.

title: Immigration and Naturalization Service v. Chadha
text:
Statutes at issue

War Powers Resolution. Undercut Sec. 5(c), which provides for withdrawal of forces by concurrent resolution.
National Emergencies Act. Undercut termination of emergencies by concurrent resolution; Congress substituted a joint resolution in 1985.
Arms Export Control Act. Undercut the concurrent resolution of disapproval for arms sales; Congress substituted a joint resolution in 1986.

Studied in Unit 1: Where the power comes from.

title: United States v. Curtiss-Wright Export Corp.
text:
Supreme Court 299 U.S. 304 Decided December 21, 1936 7 to 1
Holding. Upheld the delegation. Because foreign affairs powers rest on national sovereignty rather than on the Constitution’s specific grants alone, Congress may give the President broader discretion abroad than at home.
Question. Whether a 1934 joint resolution letting the President ban arms sales to the countries fighting the Chaco War, Bolivia and Paraguay, was an unconstitutional delegation of legislative power.
Background reading: Wikipedia article on Curtiss-Wright (secondary source).

title: United States v. Curtiss-Wright Export Corp.
text:
Why it matters
The most cited case for executive power in foreign affairs, chiefly for Justice Sutherland’s description of the President as the “sole organ of the federal government in the field of international relations.” That language was not needed to decide the case, and executive branch lawyers have long relied on it. Its delegation holding underpins the broad discretion Congress grants in statutes such as the IEEPA and the Arms Export Control Act.

title: United States v. Curtiss-Wright Export Corp.
text:
Status
The delegation holding remains good law. In Zivotofsky v. Kerry the Court declined to read the “sole organ” language as establishing exclusive presidential power in foreign affairs.

title: United States v. Curtiss-Wright Export Corp.
text:
Statutes at issue

Constitution (war powers). Treated the foreign affairs power as an attribute of national sovereignty, supporting broad delegations to the President.

Studied in Unit 1: Where the power comes from.
See this case in the knowledge graph

title: United States v. Curtiss-Wright Export Corp.
text:
Sources

Opinion (official): 299 U.S. 304
Background (secondary): Wikipedia, United States v. Curtiss-Wright Export Corp.

title: Hamdan v. Rumsfeld
text:
Supreme Court 548 U.S. 557 Decided June 29, 2006 5 to 3
Holding. No. The commissions’ procedures violated the Uniform Code of Military Justice, which requires that commission rules match those of courts-martial as far as practicable, and Common Article 3 of the Geneva Conventions. The Detainee Treatment Act’s jurisdiction-stripping provision did not apply to pending cases.
Question. Whether the military commissions the President established by order to try Guantanamo detainees were lawful.
Background reading: Wikipedia article on Hamdan (secondary source).

title: Hamdan v. Rumsfeld
text:
Why it matters
Hamdan made the scope of statutory authority, not inherent power, the decisive question, and so gave Congress the next move. It also confirmed that Common Article 3 applies to the conflict with al-Qaeda, which shaped detention and interrogation policy.

title: Hamdan v. Rumsfeld
text:
How Congress responded
Within four months Congress enacted the Military Commissions Act, authorizing commissions by statute and barring habeas petitions from Guantanamo detainees, a provision later struck down in Boumediene.

title: Hamdan v. Rumsfeld
text:
Status
Good law as to its statutory holdings; the commissions now rest on the 2006 act as amended in 2009.

title: Hamdan v. Rumsfeld
text:
Statutes at issue

UCMJ. Held the commissions failed the UCMJ’s requirement that their procedures be uniform with courts-martial as far as practicable.
Detainee Treatment Act. Held its bar on habeas jurisdiction did not reach cases already pending.

Studied in Unit 3: Deciding to use force.

text:

Background (secondary): Wikipedia, Hamdan v. Rumsfeld

title: Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project
text:
Supreme Court 561 U.S. 1 Decided June 21, 2010 6 to 3
Holding. Yes, as applied to the plaintiffs’ proposed activities. The ban in 18 U.S.C. 2339B is not unconstitutionally vague and does not violate the First Amendment, given Congress’s and the executive’s judgment that any support frees resources for terrorism.
Question. Whether the federal ban on providing material support to designated foreign terrorist organizations could be applied to training, expert advice, and other support intended only to promote the groups’ lawful, nonviolent activities.
Background reading: Wikipedia article on Humanitarian Law Project (secondary source).

title: Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project
text:
Why it matters
The Court deferred heavily to the political branches’ national security judgments while applying demanding First Amendment scrutiny, a combination often cited in later cases. It confirmed the reach of the material-support offense the AEDPA (terrorism) created, which is the main criminal tool tied to foreign terrorist organization designations.

title: Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project
text:
Status
Good law.

title: Holder v. Humanitarian Law Project
text:
Statutes at issue

AEDPA (terrorism). Upheld the material-support ban in 18 U.S.C. 2339B, enacted by the act, against vagueness and First Amendment challenges as applied.

Studied in Unit 5: Emergency and economic powers.

title: Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump
text:
Supreme Court 607 U.S. ___ Decided February 20, 2026 6 to 3
Holding. No. IEEPA does not authorize the President to impose tariffs. The Court affirmed the Federal Circuit’s judgment against the tariffs in the companion case and ordered the challenge brought in district court dismissed for lack of jurisdiction.
Question. Whether the International Emergency Economic Powers Act authorizes the President to impose tariffs, as he did in 2025 after declaring national emergencies over drug trafficking and trade deficits.
Background reading: Wikipedia article on Learning Resources v. Trump (secondary source).

title: Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump
text:
Why it matters
The decision limits the IEEPA to its traditional tools, blocking and regulating transactions, and reaffirms that the taxing power, including tariffs, belongs to Congress unless it clearly delegates it. The sanctions programs built on IEEPA were not at issue. Tariffs now depend on statutes that expressly authorize them, such as Section 232.

title: Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump
text:
How Congress responded
As of November 2026 Congress had not legislated on the question. The administration turned the same day to other tariff authorities, including Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974.

title: Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump
text:
Status
Good law; decided February 20, 2026.

title: Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump
text:
Statutes at issue

IEEPA. Held that the act’s authority to regulate importation does not include the power to impose tariffs.

Studied in Unit 5: Emergency and economic powers.
See this case in the knowledge graph

title: Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump
text:
Sources

Background (secondary): Wikipedia, Learning Resources, Inc. v. Trump

title: Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer
text:
Supreme Court 343 U.S. 579 Decided June 2, 1952 6 to 3
Holding. Held the seizure unlawful. No statute authorized it, and the President’s powers as Commander in Chief and chief executive did not extend to taking private property at home to settle a labor dispute; that was lawmaking reserved to Congress.
Question. Whether President Truman, to avert a strike during the Korean War, could seize the nation’s steel mills without statutory authority.
Background reading: Wikipedia article on Youngstown (secondary source).

title: Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer
text:
Why it matters
Justice Jackson’s concurrence supplies the framework courts and executive branch lawyers still use. Presidential power is at its maximum when the President acts with Congress’s express or implied authorization, in a “zone of twilight” when Congress has said nothing, and at its “lowest ebb” when the President acts against Congress’s will. Much of this wiki can be read through it: an AUMF puts the President in the first category, and the War Powers Resolution and funding limits like the Case-Church Amendment are attempts to push contrary action into the third. The majority noted that the Selective Service Act and the Defense Production Act let the President take property under conditions the government conceded were not met, and Justice Frankfurter’s concurrence traced how Congress had withheld seizure power in 1947.

title: Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer
text:
Status
Good law. Jackson’s concurrence, rather than the majority opinion, is the controlling framework in later cases such as Dames & Moore and Zivotofsky v. Kerry.

title: Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer
text:
Statutes at issue

Constitution (war powers). Held that the Commander in Chief and executive powers did not authorize a domestic seizure of private property without Congress.
Defense Production Act. Its property-taking provisions in Title II did not support the seizure; the government conceded their conditions were not met, and the concurrences found no implied seizure power in the act.
Selective Service Act. Its authority to seize plants under certain conditions did not support the seizure; the government conceded the conditions were not met.

Studied in Unit 1: Where the power comes from.

text:
Sources

Opinion (official): 343 U.S. 579
Background (secondary): Wikipedia, Youngstown Sheet & Tube Co. v. Sawyer

title: Atomic Energy Act of 1954
text:
In force Framework statute Pub. L. 83-703 68 Stat. 919 42 U.S.C. 2011 et seq.
The governing law for both civilian and military uses of nuclear material in the United States. It keeps nuclear weapons under civilian control, creates a separate classification regime for nuclear information, and sets the terms for nuclear cooperation with other countries.

title: Atomic Energy Act of 1954
text:
Key provisions

Restricted Data: nuclear weapons design information is classified from creation, outside the ordinary executive order system.
Sec. 123: agreements for peaceful nuclear cooperation must meet nine nonproliferation criteria and lie before Congress for review.
Secs. 91 and 144: military applications and defense cooperation with allies.
Sec. 57b: controls on assistance to foreign nuclear programs.
Sec. 135: congressional review of nuclear agreements with Iran.

title: Atomic Energy Act of 1954
text:
Why it matters
Every civil nuclear deal, from India in 2008 to current proposals in the Gulf, is a ‘Section 123’ question. Naval reactor cooperation under AUKUS runs through its defense provisions. The Iran Nuclear Review Act amended it and the Symington-Glenn Amendments reinforce it from the aid side.

title: Atomic Energy Act of 1954
text:
Current status
In force as amended, notably by the Nuclear Non-Proliferation Act of 1978 (Pub. L. 95-242).
Last checked November 10, 2026.

title: Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996
text:
In force Specific authorization Pub. L. 104-132 110 Stat. 1214 8 U.S.C. 1189; 18 U.S.C. 2339B
Passed after the Oklahoma City bombing. Its national security significance lies in two linked provisions: the Secretary of State’s power to designate foreign terrorist organizations, and the crime of giving such organizations material support.

title: Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996
text:
Key provisions

Sec. 302 (8 U.S.C. 1189): designation of foreign terrorist organizations by the Secretary of State.
Sec. 303 (18 U.S.C. 2339B): criminal ban on knowingly providing material support or resources to a designated organization.
Removed sovereign immunity for state sponsors of terrorism in certain suits by victims.
Also restricted federal habeas corpus review, a domestic matter outside this wiki’s scope.

title: Antiterrorism and Effective Death Penalty Act of 1996

title: Antideficiency Act
text:
In force Framework statute 33 Stat. 1257 31 U.S.C. 1341-1342, 1349-1351, 1511-1519
The fiscal law that makes the purse enforceable. Federal officials may not spend or obligate more than Congress has appropriated, may not commit the government to pay before an appropriation is made, and may not accept voluntary services. Violations must be reported to the President, Congress, and the Comptroller General and can bring discipline or criminal penalties.

title: Antideficiency Act
text:
Key provisions

31 U.S.C. 1341(a): no obligation or expenditure exceeding, or in advance of, an appropriation, unless authorized by law.
31 U.S.C. 1342: no voluntary services, except in emergencies involving the safety of human life or the protection of property; the legal basis for which work continues during a lapse in appropriations.
31 U.S.C. 1512-1513: the President apportions appropriations, and reserves may be set only for contingencies, savings, or as provided by law.
31 U.S.C. 1349-1350 and 1517(b): administrative discipline, criminal penalties for knowing and willful violations, and mandatory reports of every violation.
31 U.S.C. 1341(c): back pay for employees furloughed or required to work during a lapse in appropriations beginning on or after December 22, 2018.

title: Antideficiency Act
text:
Why it matters
Shutdowns run on this act: without an appropriation, agencies stop all work except what the emergency exception and other law allow. It is also the enforcement backstop for transfer limits such as Sec. 8005 transfers and for the purpose statute (31 U.S.C. 1301(a)), which allows appropriations to be used only for the purposes for which they were made. Apportionment, the step where the Office of Management and Budget releases funds to agencies, connects it to the Impoundment Control Act. The core rules date to an 1870 statute, strengthened in 1905 and 1906.

title: Antideficiency Act
text:
Current status
In force. The current text is in Title 31, restated without substantive change in 1982 (Pub. L. 97-258) and amended since, most recently to guarantee back pay after a lapse in appropriations.
Last checked November 24, 2026.

text:
Repealed Specific authorization Pub. L. 102-1 105 Stat. 3 50 U.S.C. 1541 note
Authorized the President to use force under U.N. Security Council Resolution 678 to expel Iraqi forces from Kuwait, after a presidential determination that diplomatic means had been exhausted.

title: Authorization for Use of Military Force Against Iraq Resolution (1991)
text:

title: Boland Amendments
text:
Lapsed Targeted provision Pub. L. 98-473 98 Stat. 1935
A series of appropriations limits on U.S. support for the Contras fighting Nicaragua’s government. The first, in December 1982 (in Pub. L. 97-377), barred funds for the purpose of overthrowing that government. The strictest, Sec. 8066 of Pub. L. 98-473 (October 1984), barred the CIA, the Defense Department, and any other agency involved in intelligence activities from spending funds during fiscal year 1985 to support military or paramilitary operations in Nicaragua, directly or indirectly.

title: Boland Amendments
text:
Key provisions

Sec. 8066(a) (FY1985): no funds available to the CIA, the Defense Department, or any intelligence entity for direct or indirect support of military or paramilitary operations in Nicaragua.
Sec. 8066(b): the bar could lift after February 28, 1985 only on a presidential report and a joint resolution approving further support.
Named for Representative Edward Boland, then chairman of the House intelligence committee.

title: Boland Amendments
text:
Why it matters
The Boland Amendments show the purse used against intelligence activity rather than open war. Efforts to keep supporting the Contras outside appropriated channels led to the Iran-Contra affair, which in turn led Congress to write the statutory definition of covert action and tighten finding and notice rules in 1991 (see the National Security Act and the Intel Oversight Act). They are a standing reference point whenever a funding limit is proposed for an intelligence or special operations activity.

title: U.S. Constitution: War and Foreign Affairs Powers
text:
In force Constitution
The Constitution divides national security powers between Congress and the President and leaves the boundary largely undefined. Every statute in this wiki is an exercise of, or an argument about, one of these clauses.

title: U.S. Constitution: War and Foreign Affairs Powers
text:
Key provisions

Art. I, Sec. 8, cl. 11: Congress declares war and grants letters of marque and reprisal.
Art. I, Sec. 8, cls. 12-14: Congress raises and supports armies (with appropriations limited to two years), maintains a navy, and makes rules for the armed forces.
Art. I, Sec. 8, cls. 15-16: Congress provides for calling forth and organizing the militia.
Art. I, Sec. 8, cl. 18 and Sec. 9, cl. 7: the necessary and proper power and the requirement that money be spent only under appropriations.
Art. II, Sec. 2: the President is commander in chief, makes treaties with the consent of two thirds of the Senate, and appoints ambassadors and officers.
Art. II, Sec. 3 and Art. IV, Sec. 4: the duty to see the laws faithfully executed, and the guarantee to protect states against invasion and domestic violence.

title: U.S. Constitution: War and Foreign Affairs Powers
text:
Why it matters
The standard framework for disputes is Justice Jackson’s concurrence in Youngstown Sheet and Tube Co. v. Sawyer (1952): presidential power is strongest when Congress has authorized the action and weakest when Congress has forbidden it. That is why framework statutes such as the War Powers Resolution and the National Emergencies Act matter even when they are not enforced in court. The militia clauses are the source of the Militia Acts of 1792 and, through them, the Insurrection Act.

title: U.S. Constitution: War and Foreign Affairs Powers
text:
Current status
In force. Its allocation of war and foreign affairs powers is settled more by practice than by court rulings.
Last checked November 10, 2026.

title: U.S. Constitution: War and Foreign Affairs Powers
text:
In the courts

Curtiss-Wright (1936). Treated the foreign affairs power as an attribute of national sovereignty, supporting broad delegations to the President.
Youngstown (1952). Held that the Commander in Chief and executive powers did not authorize a domestic seizure of private property without Congress.
Zivotofsky v. Kerry (2015). Held the recognition power is exclusively the President’s, and rejected a general reading of Curtiss-Wright’s ‘sole organ’ language.

title: Declarations of War (1812-1942)
text:
In force Specific authorization
Congress has declared war eleven times, in five conflicts: the War of 1812, the Mexican-American War, the Spanish-American War, and the two world wars. Each declaration was a joint resolution or act signed by the President.

title: Declarations of War (1812-1942)
text:
Key provisions

A declaration creates a state of war under international and domestic law and authorizes the President to use the whole of the armed forces.
It automatically activates standby statutes written for ‘time of war’, covering enemy aliens, trade with the enemy, surveillance, and mobilization.
The last declarations, against Bulgaria, Hungary, and Romania, were approved on June 5, 1942.

title: Declarations of War (1812-1942)
text:
Why it matters
Since 1942 Congress has authorized force by narrower resolutions such as the 2001 AUMF, which do not trigger most wartime statutes. That is why the declared-war requirement in the Alien Enemies Act and the Trading with the Enemy Act still matters, and why Section 2(c) of the War Powers Resolution lists a declaration of war first among the grounds for using force.

title: Declarations of War (1812-1942)
text:
Current status
No declaration has been enacted since June 1942. Statutes triggered by a declared war remain on the books and would activate on a new declaration.
Last checked November 10, 2026.

title: Defense Production Act of 1950
text:
Partly expired Framework statute Pub. L. 81-774 64 Stat. 798 50 U.S.C. 4501 et seq.
A Korean War statute that lets the President direct private industry in the interest of national defense: by putting government orders first in line, by financing new production capacity, and by organizing industry cooperation.

title: Defense Production Act of 1950
text:
Key provisions

Title I: priorities and allocations, requiring companies to accept and prioritize rated orders.
Title III: loans, loan guarantees, purchase commitments, and direct investment to expand domestic production.
Title VII: voluntary agreements with industry, industrial base surveys, and Section 721 on review of foreign investment.
‘National defense’ is defined broadly to include energy, critical infrastructure, and emergency preparedness.

title: Defense Production Act of 1950
text:

Its use has widened from munitions to pandemic supplies, critical minerals, and energy. Its permanent Section 721 is the home of the Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States, rewritten by FIRRMA.

title: Defense Production Act of 1950
text:

Most authorities carry a sunset. They were extended from September 30, 2025 to January 30, 2026, then to September 30, 2026 by the FY2026 defense authorization. Whether they were extended again in fall 2026 was not confirmed at this wiki’s last review. Section 721 (foreign investment review) is permanent. Check current status.
Last checked November 10, 2026.

title: Espionage Act of 1917
text:
In force Framework statute Pub. L. 65-24 40 Stat. 217 18 U.S.C. 792-798

title: Espionage Act of 1917

title: Foreign Assistance Act of 1961
text:
In force Framework statute Pub. L. 87-195 75 Stat. 424 22 U.S.C. 2151 et seq.
The basic law of U.S. foreign aid. It separated economic from military assistance, set the purposes and conditions of each, and led President Kennedy to create the U.S. Agency for International Development by executive order two months later.

title: Foreign Assistance Act of 1961
text:
Key provisions

Part I: development assistance, including health, education, democracy, and disaster relief authorities.
Part II: security assistance, including the Economic Support Fund, military education and training, peacekeeping, and Section 506 drawdown authority.
Secs. 116 and 502B: human rights conditions on economic and security assistance.
Sec. 620 and following: country and conduct restrictions, including the Cuba embargo authority in Sec. 620(a).
Sec. 634A: advance notice to Congress before funds are reprogrammed.

title: Foreign Assistance Act of 1961
text:
Why it matters
Most later aid and security assistance law is written as an amendment or companion to this act: the Leahy Laws, the Symington-Glenn Amendments, the Hughes-Ryan Amendment, the Global Fragility Act, and the military sales side that became the Arms Export Control Act. Its age and accumulated amendments are a common argument for rewriting it.

title: Foreign Assistance Act of 1961

title: Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978
text:
Partly expired Framework statute Pub. L. 95-511 92 Stat. 1783 50 U.S.C. 1801 et seq.
Created a judicial process for foreign intelligence surveillance inside the United States. The government must persuade a special court that the target is a foreign power or an agent of one before it may wiretap or search.

title: Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978
text:
Key provisions

Title I: electronic surveillance orders from the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court on probable cause that the target is a foreign power or its agent.
Title III (1994): physical searches. Title IV (1998): pen registers and trap-and-trace devices. Title V (1998): business records.
Minimization procedures limit retention and sharing of information about U.S. persons.
Declared to be the exclusive means for covered foreign intelligence surveillance.

title: Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978
text:

title: Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Act of 1978

title: Foreign Military Financing (Arms Export Control Act, Sec. 23)
text:
In force Targeted provision Pub. L. 90-629 82 Stat. 1324 22 U.S.C. 2763
The main U.S. program that pays for foreign governments’ purchases of American weapons, services, and training. Section 23 of the Arms Export Control Act authorizes the President to finance partners’ procurement; the annual appropriations act provides the money, mostly as grants, and partners usually spend it through Foreign Military Sales.

title: Foreign Military Financing (Arms Export Control Act, Sec. 23)
text:
Key provisions

Sec. 23(a): authority to finance procurement of defense articles, defense services, and design and construction services by friendly countries and international organizations.
Sec. 23(a): limited authority to finance commercial leases of defense articles for Israel and Egypt.
Sec. 23(b)-(c): for loans, repayment within 12 years unless a statute allows longer, and interest rules.
Annual appropriations add conditions, including notice to the Appropriations Committees before committing funds for major defense equipment beyond what was justified.
Recipients remain subject to Leahy Laws vetting and the coup restriction.

title: Foreign Military Financing (Arms Export Control Act, Sec. 23)
text:
Why it matters
FMF is the largest U.S. security assistance grant program, and a few partners, above all Israel and Egypt, have historically received most of it. Because it is State Department money spent on Defense Department sales, it sits at the center of the Title 22 security assistance system, in contrast to the Defense Department’s own Title 10 security cooperation authorities. Country allocations, earmarks, and conditions in the appropriations act are where Congress shapes it.

title: Foreign Military Financing (Arms Export Control Act, Sec. 23)

title: Foreign Claims Act
text:
In force Targeted provision 55 Stat. 880 10 U.S.C. 2734
Lets the military departments appoint claims commissions to settle claims by inhabitants of foreign countries for property loss, injury, or death caused by U.S. forces or incident to their noncombat activities abroad. The statute states its purpose as promoting and maintaining friendly relations through the prompt settlement of meritorious claims.

title: Foreign Claims Act
text:
Key provisions

10 U.S.C. 2734(a): claims commissions may settle foreign claims for property loss, personal injury, or death caused by, or incident to noncombat activities of, the armed forces outside the United States.
10 U.S.C. 2734(b)(1): a claim must be presented within two years after it accrues.
10 U.S.C. 2734(b)(3): no claim may arise from enemy action or result directly or indirectly from combat by U.S. forces, apart from certain aircraft accidents or malfunctions.
10 U.S.C. 2734(d): for a meritorious claim above $100,000, the department may pay $100,000 and refer the rest to the Treasury for payment.

title: Foreign Claims Act
text:
Why it matters
The combat exclusion is the gap that shapes the rest of the civilian harm framework. People harmed in combat operations cannot claim under this act, so the military relied for decades on discretionary condolence payments and now on the statutory ex gratia authority, which by its terms applies only where harm is not compensable under this act.

title: Foreign Claims Act
text:
Current status
In force. Restated in 1943 and codified in Title 10 in 1956. It does not cover harm caused by combat, which is why Congress later created a separate ex gratia authority.
Last checked November 10, 2026.

title: Global Fragility Act of 2019
text:
Partly expired Specific authorization Pub. L. 116-94 133 Stat. 2534 22 U.S.C. 9801 et seq.
Enacted as Title V of Division J of the Further Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2020. It directs a ten-year, whole-of-government strategy to prevent violent conflict and stabilize fragile states, applied first in a small set of priority countries.

title: Global Fragility Act of 2019
text:
Key provisions

Sec. 504: a Global Fragility Strategy, issued in 2020 as the U.S. Strategy to Prevent Conflict and Promote Stability.
Sec. 505: selection of priority countries and regions. In 2022 these were Haiti, Libya, Mozambique, Papua New Guinea, and Coastal West Africa (Benin, Cote d’Ivoire, Ghana, Guinea, Togo).
Sec. 506: ten-year country plans, with biennial reports to Congress.
Sec. 509: the Prevention and Stabilization Fund and the Complex Crises Fund.
State leads policy, USAID leads implementation, and Defense supports.

title: Global Fragility Act of 2019
text:
Why it matters
It is the main statutory expression of conflict prevention as a U.S. foreign policy goal and of long time horizons in assistance planning. It sits with the Elie Wiesel Act and the Women, Peace & Security Act as a set of prevention statutes, and it draws on funding authorities in the Foreign Assistance Act.

title: Global Fragility Act of 2019
text:
Current status
The policy framework remains in law, but the funding authorizations ran through fiscal year 2024. Reauthorization bills (H.R. 3005 and S. 2678, 119th Congress) were introduced in 2025 and had not been enacted as of this wiki’s last review. Implementation largely stalled in 2025 after USAID and the State Department’s conflict and stabilization bureau were dismantled.
Last checked November 10, 2026.

title: Goldwater-Nichols Department of Defense Reorganization Act of 1986
text:
In force Framework statute Pub. L. 99-433 100 Stat. 992 10 U.S.C. 151 et seq.
The most important reorganization of the Defense Department since 1947. It took operational control away from the service chiefs, ran the chain of command from the President through the Secretary of Defense to the combatant commanders, and made the Chairman of the Joint Chiefs the principal military adviser.

title: Goldwater-Nichols Department of Defense Reorganization Act of 1986
text:
Key provisions

Chain of command: President to Secretary of Defense to combatant commanders, bypassing the service chiefs.
The Chairman of the Joint Chiefs advises in his own right; the position of Vice Chairman was created.
The services organize, train, and equip forces but do not command them in operations.
Joint duty assignment made a requirement for promotion to general or flag rank.
Sec. 603: requires the President’s annual National Security Strategy report.

title: Goldwater-Nichols Department of Defense Reorganization Act of 1986
text:

It was a response to the failures of interservice coordination in the Iran hostage rescue attempt and Grenada. It amends the National Security Act and was followed weeks later by the Nunn-Cohen Amendment. Proposals for a ‘Goldwater-Nichols for the interagency’ use it as shorthand for forcing joint action by statute.

title: International Emergency Economic Powers Act
text:
In force Framework statute Pub. L. 95-223 91 Stat. 1625 50 U.S.C. 1701 et seq.
The workhorse of U.S. economic sanctions. After declaring a national emergency over an unusual and extraordinary threat that originates largely abroad, the President may block property and prohibit transactions involving foreign countries, entities, and individuals.

title: International Emergency Economic Powers Act
text:
Key provisions

Sec. 202: requires a declared national emergency specific to the threat.
Sec. 203: power to investigate, block, regulate, or prohibit transactions and property subject to U.S. jurisdiction.
Sec. 203(b): exceptions for personal communications, humanitarian donations, informational materials, and travel.
Sec. 204: consultation with and reporting to Congress.
Sec. 206: civil and criminal penalties, raised substantially in 2007.

title: International Emergency Economic Powers Act
text:
Why it matters
Almost every program administered by the Treasury Department’s Office of Foreign Assets Control rests on it, each tied to an emergency under the National Emergencies Act. Statutory sanctions such as the Global Magnitsky Act and CAATSA are implemented through its machinery. After the 2026 tariff ruling, trade measures shifted to other authorities such as Section 232.

title: International Emergency Economic Powers Act
text:

title: International Emergency Economic Powers Act
text:

title: Impoundment Control Act of 1974
text:
In force Framework statute Pub. L. 93-344 88 Stat. 332 2 U.S.C. 681-688
Title X of the Congressional Budget and Impoundment Control Act of 1974. It requires the President to spend appropriated funds unless Congress agrees otherwise. A proposal to cancel funds (a rescission) must go to Congress, and the funds must be released if Congress does not pass a rescission bill within 45 days of continuous session; delays (deferrals) are allowed only for limited reasons and not past the end of the fiscal year.

title: Impoundment Control Act of 1974
text:
Key provisions

Sec. 1001: the act does not concede or assert the constitutional powers of either branch.
Sec. 1012: special message proposing a rescission; funds must be made available unless Congress completes a rescission bill within 45 days.
Sec. 1013: deferrals only for contingencies, savings from efficiency, or as specifically provided by law, and not beyond the fiscal year.
Secs. 1014-1015: reports to Congress and the Comptroller General, who reports impoundments the President has not.
Sec. 1016: the Comptroller General may sue to release withheld funds after notice to Congress.

title: Impoundment Control Act of 1974
text:
Why it matters
Passed after the Nixon administration withheld billions in appropriated funds, the act is the main statutory check on the executive declining to spend. It works alongside the apportionment rules in the Antideficiency Act: reserves set aside in apportionment must be reported under this act. The Supreme Court’s Train v. New York decided a Nixon-era impoundment as a matter of the underlying statute. Its procedures have become central again since 2025, especially for foreign assistance funded in the State-foreign operations act.

title: Impoundment Control Act of 1974
text:
Current status
In force and contested. In July 2025 Congress enacted a rescission bill the President proposed under the act (Rescissions Act of 2025, Pub. L. 119-28), which cancelled foreign assistance and other funds. In August 2025 the President proposed rescinding further foreign assistance funds so late in the fiscal year that they would expire before the 45-day period ran out, a so-called pocket rescission. GAO has said the act does not permit this; in September 2025 the Supreme Court, on an emergency application (No. 25A269), allowed the funds to be withheld while litigation continued. Check current status.
Last checked November 24, 2026.

title: Impoundment Control Act of 1974
text:
In the courts

Train v. New York (1975). Decided under the earlier water pollution statute, the case is the judicial counterpart to the act Congress passed while it was pending.

title: Insurrection Act
text:
In force Framework statute 2 Stat. 443 10 U.S.C. 251-255
A set of provisions, first enacted in 1807 and broadened in 1861 and 1871, that lets the President use the armed forces and federalized militia inside the United States to suppress insurrection, enforce federal law, or protect civil rights when ordinary enforcement fails.

title: Insurrection Act
text:
Key provisions

10 U.S.C. 251: deployment at the request of a state legislature or governor.
10 U.S.C. 252: deployment to enforce federal law when unlawful obstruction or rebellion makes ordinary enforcement impracticable.
10 U.S.C. 253: deployment to protect constitutional rights that a state cannot or will not protect.
10 U.S.C. 254: requires a proclamation ordering insurgents to disperse before forces are used.

title: Insurrection Act
text:
Why it matters
It is the main statutory exception to the Posse Comitatus Act. A 2006 expansion made through that year’s defense authorization was repealed in 2008, and reform proposals since 2020 have focused on defining its triggers and adding time limits and judicial review.

title: Leahy Laws
text:
In force Targeted provision 22 U.S.C. 2378d; 10 U.S.C. 362
Two parallel provisions that bar U.S. assistance to any unit of a foreign security force when there is credible information that the unit committed a gross violation of human rights. They began as an appropriations rider sponsored by Senator Patrick Leahy.

title: Leahy Laws
text:
Key provisions

22 U.S.C. 2378d: no assistance under the Foreign Assistance Act or Arms Export Control Act to a tainted unit.
10 U.S.C. 362: no Defense Department training, equipment, or other assistance to a tainted unit.
Assistance can resume if the foreign government is taking effective steps to bring those responsible to justice.
Requires a vetting process and, for the State Department law, notice to the foreign government.

title: Leahy Laws
text:
Why it matters
They operate at the level of the unit, which lets the United States keep working with a country while excluding specific battalions. They constrain assistance under the Foreign Assistance Act, the Arms Export Control Act, and the Defense Department programs in Chapter 16 of Title 10. Consistency of application across recipients is the usual criticism.

title: Leahy Laws
text:
Current status
In force. The State Department version is Section 620M of the Foreign Assistance Act; the Defense Department version was made permanent in Title 10 in 2014.
Last checked November 10, 2026.

title: Logan Act
text:
In force Targeted provision 1 Stat. 613 18 U.S.C. 953
Bars private citizens from corresponding with a foreign government, without authority, in order to influence its conduct in a dispute with the United States or to defeat U.S. measures.

title: Logan Act
text:
Key provisions

Applies to any U.S. citizen acting without the authority of the United States.
Covers correspondence or intercourse with a foreign government or its agents.
Requires intent to influence that government’s conduct in a dispute with the United States, or to defeat U.S. measures.

title: Logan Act
text:
Why it matters

It expresses the principle that the government speaks with one voice abroad, and it is the diplomatic counterpart of the Neutrality Act. Modern concerns about foreign influence are handled through FARA instead.

title: Militia Acts of 1792
text:
Superseded Framework statute 1 Stat. 264; 1 Stat. 271 10 U.S.C. 246
Two acts passed a week apart. The first let the President call out state militias to repel invasion, suppress insurrection, and enforce federal law. The second required the states to enroll and organize a militia of adult male citizens.

title: Militia Acts of 1792
text:
Key provisions

Calling Forth Act (May 2, 1792): presidential authority to call the militia in case of invasion, insurrection, or obstruction of the laws, at first only after a federal judge certified the need.
Required a proclamation ordering insurgents to disperse before force was used.
Uniform Militia Act (May 8, 1792): enrollment of able-bodied free white male citizens aged 18 to 45, who were to arm themselves.

title: Militia Acts of 1792
text:
Why it matters
This was Congress’s first delegation of its militia power, used by Washington in the Whiskey Rebellion. The dispersal proclamation and the three triggers carry straight through to the Insurrection Act and to Section 12406 in the mobilization authorities. Its failure as a system for organizing forces led to the Militia Act of 1903.

title: Militia Acts of 1792
text:
Current status
Replaced in stages by the Militia Act of 1795, the Insurrection Act of 1807, and the Militia Act of 1903. The statutory definition of the militia survives at 10 U.S.C. 246.
Last checked November 10, 2026.

title: National Defense Authorization Act (annual series)
text:
In force Specific authorization Title 10 U.S.C. (various)
The annual law that authorizes funding levels and sets policy for the Defense Department and the nuclear weapons programs of the Energy Department. It has been enacted every year for more than six decades, which makes it the most reliable vehicle in Congress for national security legislation of all kinds.

title: National Defense Authorization Act (annual series)
text:
Key provisions

Authorizes appropriations for procurement, research, operations, personnel, and military construction; actual funding comes from separate appropriations acts.
Sets personnel policy, including pay, end strength, and military justice.
Creates, extends, and limits security cooperation and counterterrorism authorities.
Routinely carries unrelated or loosely related titles, such as the intelligence and State Department authorizations and sanctions measures.

title: National Defense Authorization Act (annual series)
text:
Why it matters
Much of this wiki passed through it. It carried the Global Magnitsky Act, the Caesar Act, the Export Control Reform Act, FIRRMA, Chapter 16 of Title 10, and the Nunn-Cohen Amendment, and the FY2026 act repealed the 2002 Iraq AUMF and the 1991 Gulf War AUMF. Knowing which year’s act did what is often the fastest way to trace a provision.

title: Neutrality Act of 1794
text:
In force Framework statute 1 Stat. 381 18 U.S.C. 958-962
Makes it a crime for private persons to wage war from U.S. territory against a country with which the United States is at peace. It was passed to keep Americans from dragging the country into the wars of the French Revolution.

title: Neutrality Act of 1794
text:

18 U.S.C. 960: organizing or funding a military expedition from the United States against a friendly foreign state.

title: Neutrality Act of 1794
text:
Why it matters
It establishes that the decision to use force abroad belongs to the government and not to private citizens. The Logan Act applies the same idea to diplomacy, and the Espionage Act added to its enforcement provisions. It is distinct from the arms embargo laws of the 1930s that share its name.

title: National Security Act Amendments of 1949
text:
In force Framework statute Pub. L. 81-216 63 Stat. 578 10 U.S.C. 111, 151
Fixed the weak structure created in 1947. It turned the National Military Establishment into the Department of Defense, an executive department, and reduced the Army, Navy, and Air Force to military departments under the Secretary of Defense.

title: National Security Act Amendments of 1949
text:
Key provisions

Created the Department of Defense as an executive department.
Removed the service secretaries from the cabinet and from the National Security Council.
Created the position of Chairman of the Joint Chiefs of Staff, without command authority.
Added a deputy secretary and comptroller and gave the Secretary control of the budget.

title: National Security Act Amendments of 1949
text:

It is the first of three corrections to the National Security Act, followed by the DoD Reorganization Act (1958) and the Goldwater-Nichols Act, each of which moved authority from the services toward the Secretary and joint commanders.

title: Presidential Drawdown Authority (Foreign Assistance Act, Sec. 506)
text:
In force Targeted provision Pub. L. 87-195 75 Stat. 437 22 U.S.C. 2318
Lets the President send weapons, equipment, services, and training from existing Defense Department stocks to a foreign country in an emergency or for listed purposes, without a new appropriation. Replacing what is drawn down takes separate appropriations, which is why large drawdowns are usually paired with supplemental funding.

title: Presidential Drawdown Authority (Foreign Assistance Act, Sec. 506)
text:
Key provisions

Sec. 506(a)(1): up to $100 million a year in defense articles, services, and training for an unforeseen emergency that cannot be met under the Arms Export Control Act or other law.
Sec. 506(a)(2): up to $200 million a year, from any agency, for counternarcotics, disaster relief, antiterrorism, nonproliferation, refugee assistance, and cooperation with Vietnam, Cambodia, and Laos on U.S. personnel missing from the Vietnam War.
Each drawdown rests on a presidential determination reported to Congress.

title: Presidential Drawdown Authority (Foreign Assistance Act, Sec. 506)
text:
Why it matters
Drawdown is the fastest way to arm a partner because the equipment already exists. It carried most early U.S. military aid to Ukraine after February 2022, and its use there raised standing questions about the pace of replenishment, the effect on U.S. readiness, and how Congress tracks value drawn from stocks. Its contrast is Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative, which buys new equipment instead.

title: Presidential Drawdown Authority (Foreign Assistance Act, Sec. 506)
text:

title: Presidential Drawdown Authority (Foreign Assistance Act, Sec. 506)
text:

Account. None for the articles, which come from existing stocks; replacement is funded later, replacement through Defense appropriations, often in supplementals in the Defense appropriations (annual).
Run by. The Defense Department, which executes drawdowns, with the State Department coordinating policy.
Committees. Authorizing, House Foreign Affairs and Senate Foreign Relations; replacement funds, the House and Senate Defense appropriations subcommittees.

title: Posse Comitatus Act
text:

A one-sentence criminal statute that bars using federal military forces to execute the laws unless the Constitution or an act of Congress expressly authorizes it.

title: Posse Comitatus Act
text:

title: Posse Comitatus Act

title: Coup Restriction (State-Foreign Operations Appropriations, Sec. 7008)
text:
In force Targeted provision Pub. L. 119-75 140 Stat. 539
Bars the use of foreign assistance funds to finance assistance directly to the government of a country whose duly elected head of government is deposed by a military coup or decree, or by a coup or decree in which the military plays a decisive role. Aid may resume when the Secretary of State certifies that a democratically elected government has taken office.

title: Coup Restriction (State-Foreign Operations Appropriations, Sec. 7008)
text:
Key provisions

Sec. 7008(a): the prohibition, covering funds in Titles III through VI of the act, including security assistance.
Exceptions for assistance to promote democratic elections, public participation in democratic processes, or a democratic transition, with prior consultation with the Appropriations Committees.
Resumption on certification by the Secretary of State that a democratically elected government has taken office.
Sec. 7008(b) (FY2026): the Secretary may waive the restriction program by program on certifying that a waiver is in the national security interest.

title: Coup Restriction (State-Foreign Operations Appropriations, Sec. 7008)
text:
Why it matters
The restriction is triggered by the facts, but in practice by a formal determination that a coup occurred, which makes the determination itself a recurring oversight question. Administrations have at times avoided one, as with Egypt in 2013; in October 2023 the State Department determined that the July takeover in Niger was a coup and suspended most assistance under this section. It reaches programs funded through the State-foreign operations act, such as Foreign Military Financing and IMET, but not Defense Department authorities such as Title 10 security cooperation unless a separate law applies.

title: State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs Appropriations Act (annual series)
text:
In force Specific authorization Pub. L. 119-75 140 Stat. 513
The annual law that funds the State Department and foreign assistance, including the security assistance accounts that pay for Foreign Military Financing, IMET, and Peacekeeping Operations. Its general provisions, numbered from Sec. 7001, carry many of the standing conditions on foreign aid, such as the coup restriction. Foreign assistance has had its own annual appropriation since the first one under the Foreign Assistance Act, the Foreign Assistance and Related Agencies Appropriation Act, 1962 (Pub. L. 87-329).

title: State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs Appropriations Act (annual series)
text:
Key provisions

Title I: Department of State and related programs. Title II: administration of assistance. Title III: bilateral economic assistance.
Title IV: international security assistance, including International Military Education and Training, the Foreign Military Financing Program, and Peacekeeping Operations.
Titles V and VI: multilateral assistance, and export and investment assistance.
Title VII general provisions: notification of the Appropriations Committees 15 days before obligating funds beyond justified amounts, the coup restriction in Sec. 7008, and country-specific conditions.

title: State, Foreign Operations, and Related Programs Appropriations Act (annual series)
text:
Why it matters
Much foreign policy is made here rather than in authorizing law. Congress has not enacted a comprehensive foreign assistance authorization in decades, so the annual act, through its accounts, earmarks, notification rules, and conditions, is the main way it shapes aid. The Leahy Laws began as a rider to this act. For staff, the act’s general provisions and the joint explanatory statement are usually the controlling text for how a program may be run in a given year.

title: Title 10, U.S. Code: Armed Forces
text:
In force Code title overview Pub. L. 84-1028 70A Stat. 1 10 U.S.C. 101 et seq.
The title of the U.S. Code that governs the armed forces: their organization, command, personnel, training, procurement, and reserve components. Congress enacted it as positive law in 1956, so its text is itself the law and not just evidence of it.

title: Title 10, U.S. Code: Armed Forces
text:
Key provisions

Subtitle A, General Military Law: the Department of Defense, the Joint Chiefs and combatant commands, personnel, the Uniform Code of Military Justice, training, and acquisition.
Subtitle B: Army. Subtitle C: Navy and Marine Corps. Subtitle D: Air Force and Space Force.
Subtitle E: Reserve Components, including the mobilization authorities.
Key operational sections include 113 and 162-164 (command), 127e (special operations support), 251-255 (insurrection), 271-284 (support to law enforcement), 301-386 (security cooperation), and 394 (cyber).

title: Title 10, U.S. Code: Armed Forces
text:
Why it matters
‘Title 10’ is shorthand for military authority exercised through the chain of command, as opposed to intelligence authority under Title 50, diplomatic and assistance authority under Title 22, or National Guard service under Title 32. Its structure was set by the National Security Act and its amendments, and nearly all changes now come through the annual NDAA.

title: Title 32, U.S. Code: National Guard
text:
In force Code title overview Pub. L. 84-1028 70A Stat. 596 32 U.S.C. 101 et seq.
The title of the U.S. Code for the National Guard when it is not in federal service. It governs organization, federal funding, and training of the Guard while it remains under the command of state governors.

title: Title 32, U.S. Code: National Guard
text:
Key provisions

Federal recognition, organization, and equipment standards for the Guard.
Sec. 502(f): Guard members may perform training or other duty, including operational support requested by the President or Secretary of Defense, while under state command and federally paid.
Sec. 112: counterdrug support under governors’ plans.
Chapter 9: homeland defense activities.

title: Title 32, U.S. Code: National Guard
text:
Why it matters
‘Title 32 status’ is the middle position between purely state service and federal service under Title 10: federal money and missions, state command. Because troops in that status are not federal forces, the Posse Comitatus Act does not apply to them, which is why the choice of status under the mobilization authorities is often the decisive legal question in domestic deployments. Its roots are in the Militia Act of 1903.

title: Gulf of Tonkin Resolution
text:
Repealed Specific authorization Pub. L. 88-408 78 Stat. 384
A joint resolution approving ‘all necessary measures’ by the President to repel attacks on U.S. forces and prevent further aggression in Southeast Asia. It became the legal foundation for the escalation of the Vietnam War.

title: Gulf of Tonkin Resolution
text:
Key provisions

Approved and supported the President’s determination to take all necessary measures to repel armed attack and prevent further aggression.
Authorized force to assist any member or protocol state of the Southeast Asia Collective Defense Treaty that requested help.
Would expire when the President determined peace was secured, or earlier by concurrent resolution of Congress.

title: Gulf of Tonkin Resolution
text:
Why it matters
Its open-ended wording, and later doubts about the incident that prompted it, shaped the congressional backlash that produced the War Powers Resolution and the wider reassertion statutes of the 1970s.

text:
In force Framework statute Pub. L. 65-91 40 Stat. 411 50 U.S.C. 4301-4341

title: War Powers Resolution
text:
In force Framework statute Pub. L. 93-148 87 Stat. 555 50 U.S.C. 1541-1550
Passed over President Nixon’s veto, the War Powers Resolution is Congress’s framework statute for sharing the decision to commit U.S. forces to hostilities. It requires consultation before forces are introduced, a report to Congress within 48 hours, and withdrawal within 60 days (plus a 30-day drawdown) unless Congress declares war or passes a specific authorization.

title: War Powers Resolution
text:
Key provisions

Sec. 2(c): states that the President may introduce forces into hostilities only under a declaration of war, specific statutory authorization, or a national emergency created by an attack on the United States.
Sec. 3: consultation with Congress ‘in every possible instance’ before introducing forces.
Sec. 4(a)(1): written report within 48 hours of introducing forces into hostilities or imminent hostilities.
Sec. 5(b): the 60-day termination clock, extendable by 30 days for safe withdrawal.
Sec. 5(c): withdrawal by concurrent resolution, widely viewed as unenforceable after INS v. Chadha (1983); expedited joint-resolution procedures were added in 1983.
Sec. 8: authority to use force may not be inferred from appropriations acts or treaties.

title: War Powers Resolution
text:
Why it matters
It is the reference point for every later use-of-force debate. Each authorization for use of military force, including the 2001 AUMF, declares itself to be the ‘specific statutory authorization’ that Sec. 5(b) requires. Disputes usually turn on what counts as ‘hostilities’ and on whether a report was filed under Sec. 4(a)(1), which is what starts the clock.

title: War Powers Resolution
text:
Current status
In force. Every administration since Nixon has questioned the constitutionality of parts of it, and the 60-day clock has rarely been treated as binding. In 2026 House members introduced resolutions under it concerning U.S. military action in Venezuela and against Iran; their outcomes are not recorded here. Check current status.
Last checked November 10, 2026.

title: War Powers Resolution
text:
In the courts

INS v. Chadha (1983). Undercut Sec. 5(c), which provides for withdrawal of forces by concurrent resolution.

title: Study guide
text: This guide is for anyone learning the national security portfolio, from interns to staff taking on a new committee or issue. It answers two questions: how the laws fit together, and in what order to learn them. Work through the units in order, or go straight to the one you need before a hearing, markup, or meeting. Each unit has a reading path, key terms, Issues for Congress, and questions to check yourself. Progress you tick off is saved in your own browser only.

title: Study guide
text:
Is there a hierarchy?
Yes, in three senses, and each part of the site shows one of them.

Authority. Every statute draws on a constitutional power, and many work only through another statute. A sanctions act needs IEEPA, and IEEPA needs a national emergency declared under the National Emergencies Act. The authority stack below sorts every law in the wiki by its place in that chain. The knowledge graph’s Authority layers view draws the same stack with its connections, and each statute page lists what it builds on and what is built upon it.
Codification. Enacted laws are filed by subject into titles of the U.S. Code: Title 10 for the armed forces, Title 50 for war and national defense, Title 22 for foreign relations, Title 32 for the National Guard. The title pages and the Title 10 and Title 50 explainer show this shelf.
Time. Each generation of law answered the failures of the one before: the 1947 system, the 1970s reassertion after Vietnam and Watergate, the post-September 11 expansion, and the recent turn to sanctions, cyber, and civilian harm. The timeline groups the statutes and court decisions by era.

Two things cut across all three. Money: almost every authority here depends on an annual appropriation, and funding limits are among Congress’s strongest tools (Unit 4). The courts: Supreme Court decisions settle what the statutes mean and where presidential power runs out; Justice Jackson’s concurrence in Youngstown is the framework most often used. See the court cases.

title: Study guide
section: Using this guide in an office
text:
Using this guide in an office

Onboarding. Assign a new staffer or intern the units that match the office’s committees. Armed Services: Units 2, 3, 4, 8, 9, and 12. Foreign Affairs or Foreign Relations: Units 3, 5, 10, and 11. Intelligence: Units 6 and 7. Appropriations: Units 4, 10, and 11. Banking (sanctions and export controls): Units 5 and 11.
Briefing preparation. Before a hearing or markup, read the “Current status” and “In the courts” sections of the statute pages involved, then the unit’s Issues for Congress, which set out the main arguments on each side without taking one.
Trace a chain. Take a current event, such as a strike, a sanctions designation, an arms sale, or a Guard deployment, and trace its legal basis down the stack: which constitutional power, which framework statute, which specific authorization, which provision, and which appropriation pays for it. The graph’s Authority layers view helps.
Check yourself. Each unit ends with questions whose answers are hidden. They work for self-study or as a short quiz for an intern cohort.
Read the primary text. Every reading card links to the official text. Before quoting a provision in a memo, letter, or bill, confirm it there.
Watch the moving parts. Statutes whose status note ends “Check current status” are where the law is changing, and each page shows when it was last checked.

title: Unit 11: Arms transfers, export controls, and investment screening
text:
Previous: Unit 10. Foreign assistance, fragility, and partners | All units | Next: Unit 12. Civilian harm and the conduct of operations
The Arms Export Control Act governs weapons sales and gives Congress notice of major sales and a way to block them. Most major sales go through Foreign Military Sales, often paid for with Foreign Military Financing grants, while drawdown and the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative are the fast and slow paths for arming a partner at war. Export controls on dual-use technology now rest on the Export Control Reform Act, and foreign investment review runs through CFIUS as expanded by FIRRMA. Nonproliferation conditions and the Taiwan Relations Act show how Congress attaches policy to transfers.
