title: Unit 11: Arms transfers, export controls, and investment screening
text:
Further reading

Presidential drawdown (Sec. 506): Lets the President send weapons, equipment, services, and training from existing Defense Department stocks to a foreign country in an emergency or for listed purposes, without a new appropriation.
Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative: The Defense Department’s authority to provide security assistance and intelligence support, including training, equipment, and logistics, to Ukraine’s military and other security forces.
Excess Defense Articles: Allows the President to transfer surplus U.S. military equipment to eligible countries, by grant or sale, from existing Defense Department stocks.
Leahy Laws: Two parallel provisions that bar U.S. assistance to any unit of a foreign security force when there is credible information that the unit committed a gross violation of human rights.
Defense Production Act: A Korean War statute that lets the President direct private industry in the interest of national defense: by putting government orders first in line, by financing new production capacity, and by organizing industry cooperation.
Nunn-Lugar Act: Authorized the Defense Department to spend its own funds helping the former Soviet republics secure, transport, and dismantle nuclear, chemical, and other weapons after the Soviet collapse.
Section 232 (trade): Allows the President to restrict imports that threaten to impair national security. The Commerce Department investigates and reports, and the President then decides whether to impose tariffs, quotas, or negotiated limits.

title: Unit 11: Arms transfers, export controls, and investment screening
text:
Key terms

Congressional notification

Advance notice to Congress of a proposed major arms sale, which opens a period in which Congress may pass a joint resolution of disapproval.

Dual-use item

Goods, software, or technology with both civilian and military uses, controlled by the Commerce Department under ECRA.

CFIUS

The Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States, which reviews foreign acquisitions and investments for national security risk.

Foreign Military Sales

Government-to-government sales administered by the Defense Department, in contrast to direct commercial sales, which companies make under State Department export licenses.

Drawdown

Transfer of defense articles and services from existing U.S. stocks under Sec. 506 of the Foreign Assistance Act, replaced later with new appropriations.

title: Unit 11: Arms transfers, export controls, and investment screening
text:
Issues for Congress
Questions that recur in oversight and legislation, with the main arguments on each side. There is no answer key; they are for discussion and briefing preparation.

1. Should Congress have to approve some major arms sales instead of only being able to block them?
Under the Arms Export Control Act, Congress can stop a notified sale only by a joint resolution, which the President can veto; the 2019 resolutions on sales to Saudi Arabia and the United Arab Emirates were vetoed.

Reform proposals would require affirmative approval for some sales, for example to governments with serious human rights concerns.
Opponents argue that would politicize individual sales, slow deliveries to partners, and harm alliances and the defense industrial base.



2. How should drawdown and new procurement be balanced when arming a partner at war?
Presidential drawdown delivers existing stocks quickly; the Ukraine Security Assistance Initiative buys new equipment.

Those who emphasize drawdown stress speed when a partner is under attack.
Those who emphasize procurement stress protecting U.S. readiness and building industrial capacity.

title: Unit 11: Arms transfers, export controls, and investment screening
text:
Check yourself
Try to answer each question before opening it.






Tip1. What role does the AECA give Congress in major arms sales?





Advance notice and a procedure to block a sale by joint resolution. The act also sets the purposes for which U.S. weapons may be sold and requires licenses for commercial sales. See Arms Export Control Act.









Tip2. What statute did ECRA replace, and why?





The Export Administration Act of 1979, which had lapsed and was kept alive for years by emergency declarations. See Export Control Reform Act and IEEPA.









Tip3. What triggers the Symington and Glenn Amendments?





Trading in nuclear enrichment or reprocessing technology outside international safeguards, or testing a nuclear device, which cuts off U.S. economic and military aid. See Symington-Glenn Amendments.









Tip4. Beyond takeovers, what did FIRRMA bring under review?





Minority stakes in sensitive businesses and some real estate transactions. See FIRRMA (CFIUS).

title: Unit 12: Civilian harm and the conduct of operations
text:
Previous: Unit 11. Arms transfers, export controls, and investment screening | All units
For most of its history the United States addressed civilian harm through policy and discretionary payments, not statute. The Foreign Claims Act covers only noncombat harm. Starting in 2017, Congress wrote a framework into the annual defense authorizations: a public annual casualty report, a required civilian casualty policy with a senior official, a standing ex gratia authority for combat harm, and a Civilian Protection Center of Excellence in Title 10. The Leahy Laws apply the same logic to foreign partners. Since 2025 the main question has been how far the Defense Department may scale these programs back while the statutes remain in force.

title: Unit 12: Civilian harm and the conduct of operations
text:
Further reading

Military Commissions Act: Passed after Hamdan v. Rumsfeld struck down the commissions created by presidential order, it gave statutory authority to try alien unlawful enemy combatants by military commission and defined the offenses and procedures.
UCMJ: The criminal code and court system of the U.S. armed forces. It replaced the separate Army and Navy disciplinary codes with one law for all services, defining military offenses, the types of courts-martial, the rights of the accused, and civilian appellate review.
2001 AUMF: Enacted a week after the September 11 attacks, this joint resolution authorizes the President to use all necessary and appropriate force against the nations, organizations, or persons that planned, authorized, committed, or aided the attacks, or that harbored those who did.
Women, Peace & Security Act: Makes it U.S. policy to promote the meaningful participation of women in conflict prevention, peace negotiations, and post-conflict recovery, and requires a government-wide strategy to carry that out.
Elie Wiesel Act: Declares that preventing genocide and other atrocities is a national interest of the United States and requires the executive branch to organize, train, and report accordingly.
Arms Export Control Act: Governs U.S. arms exports. It sets the purposes for which American weapons may be sold, requires licenses for commercial sales, and gives Congress advance notice of major sales and a procedure to block them.

title: Unit 12: Civilian harm and the conduct of operations
text:
Key terms

Civilian harm mitigation and response

The Defense Department’s term, abbreviated CHMR, for preventing, mitigating, and responding to civilian casualties and other harm from military operations.

Ex gratia payment

A voluntary payment to a harmed civilian or family that does not admit legal liability. Since 2019, Sec. 1213 of the FY2020 NDAA is the sole authority for such payments for harm from the use of force.

Combat exclusion

The Foreign Claims Act’s bar on claims arising from combat, which is why combat harm needs a separate ex gratia authority.

Center of Excellence

The Civilian Protection Center of Excellence at 10 U.S.C. 184, the Department’s statutory focal point for civilian harm data, guidance, and lessons learned.

title: Unit 12: Civilian harm and the conduct of operations
text:
Issues for Congress
Questions that recur in oversight and legislation, with the main arguments on each side. There is no answer key; they are for discussion and briefing preparation.

1. Is the Defense Department meeting the civilian harm statutes?
Staffing for civilian harm functions was sharply reduced in 2025 and 2026 while 10 U.S.C. 184 and the Civilian Casualty Policy remained in force.

Those who see noncompliance argue a greatly reduced staff cannot carry out functions Congress wrote into law.
Others argue the functions can be performed by a smaller staff integrated into existing organizations.



2. Should vetting or reporting extend to how partners use U.S. weapons in combat?
The Leahy Laws address gross violations of human rights by units; proposals in recent Congresses would add reporting on partners’ compliance with the law of armed conflict.

Supporters argue the United States shares responsibility for how its weapons are used and needs information to make transfer decisions.
Opponents argue added conditions burden partners in active conflicts and duplicate existing end-use monitoring and policy reviews.

title: Unit 12: Civilian harm and the conduct of operations
text:
Check yourself
Try to answer each question before opening it.






Tip1. Why can’t someone harmed in a U.S. airstrike claim under the Foreign Claims Act?





The act excludes claims arising from enemy action or resulting directly or indirectly from U.S. combat, apart from some aircraft accidents. Combat harm is addressed through ex gratia payments instead. See Foreign Claims Act.









Tip2. What must the annual civilian casualty report include, and when is it public?





Each operation with confirmed or reasonably suspected civilian casualties, with date, location, authority used, and casualty estimates, plus reasons for discrepancies with outside reporting. The unclassified report is published when submitted unless the Secretary certifies a national security threat. See Civilian Casualty Report.









Tip3. What must the senior civilian official designated under Sec. 936 do?





Develop, coordinate, and oversee compliance with civilian casualty policy, including uniform standards for recording strikes, investigating allegations, acknowledging harm, and offering ex gratia payments. See Civilian Casualty Policy.









Tip4. Why could the Defense Department not simply abolish the Civilian Protection Center of Excellence in 2025 and 2026?





Because Congress put it in Title 10 at 10 U.S.C. 184 with specific functions, so ending it requires a change in law. The dispute became whether a sharply reduced staff still satisfies the statute. See Civilian Protection Center.









Tip5. How do the Leahy Laws relate to the civilian harm statutes?





The civilian harm statutes govern U.S. operations; the Leahy Laws condition assistance to foreign units on the absence of credible information of gross human rights violations. Bills in recent Congresses have proposed extending vetting or reporting to partners’ operations.

title: Unit 5: Emergency and economic powers
text:
Previous: Unit 4. The power of the purse | All units | Next: Unit 6. Intelligence and its oversight
Most U.S. sanctions run through a two-step framework: the National Emergencies Act sets how emergencies are declared and ended, and IEEPA supplies the economic powers once one is declared. Country-specific acts then write some programs into statute and limit the President’s ability to lift them. This is the clearest example in the wiki of the layer structure: framework statutes below, specific authorizations on top.

The workhorse of U.S. economic sanctions. After declaring a national emergency over an unusual and extraordinary threat that originates largely abroad, the President may block property and prohibit transactions involving foreign countries, entities, and individuals.

A First World War statute giving the President sweeping control over trade and property involving enemy countries and nationals.

title: Unit 5: Emergency and economic powers
text:
Further reading

Helms-Burton Act: Wrote the Cuba embargo into statute so that a President cannot lift it alone, and extended its reach to foreign companies that use property confiscated by the Cuban government.
Caesar Act: Imposed secondary sanctions on foreign persons doing business with the Assad government’s military, energy, aviation, and reconstruction sectors.
Section 232 (trade): Allows the President to restrict imports that threaten to impair national security. The Commerce Department investigates and reports, and the President then decides whether to impose tariffs, quotas, or negotiated limits.
AEDPA (terrorism): Passed after the Oklahoma City bombing. Its national security significance lies in two linked provisions: the Secretary of State’s power to designate foreign terrorist organizations, and the crime of giving such organizations material support.
Section 2808 (construction): One of the standby powers unlocked by a national emergency. When a declared war or emergency requires use of the armed forces, the Secretary of Defense may build military construction projects that Congress never authorized, using unspent military construction funds.

title: Unit 5: Emergency and economic powers
text:
Key terms

National emergency

A presidential declaration under the National Emergencies Act that unlocks standby statutory powers. The President must specify which powers are being used, and emergencies lapse unless renewed each year.

Blocking

Freezing property and interests in property within U.S. jurisdiction and prohibiting transactions in them, the core tool of IEEPA sanctions.

Secondary sanctions

Penalties on foreign persons, not just U.S. persons, for dealing with a sanctioned country or sector. The Iran Sanctions Act pioneered them.

title: Unit 5: Emergency and economic powers
text:
Issues for Congress
Questions that recur in oversight and legislation, with the main arguments on each side. There is no answer key; they are for discussion and briefing preparation.

1. Should national emergencies end automatically unless Congress approves them?
Under the National Emergencies Act, an emergency continues until the President or a joint resolution ends it, and many have lasted for decades; after INS v. Chadha, ending one over the President’s objection requires a veto-proof majority.

Reform proposals would make emergencies, or the powers they unlock, lapse after a set period unless Congress votes to continue them.
Opponents argue automatic lapse could interrupt long-running sanctions programs and give a determined minority leverage over foreign policy.



2. After Learning Resources, should Congress change how trade measures are delegated?
Learning Resources v. Trump held that the IEEPA does not authorize tariffs, but other statutes still delegate tariff authority.

Some argue Congress should require its approval for tariffs imposed under any delegated authority, reclaiming the taxing power more broadly.
Others argue statutes such as Section 232 give the executive needed flexibility to respond quickly to trade and security threats.

title: Unit 5: Emergency and economic powers
text:
Check yourself
Try to answer each question before opening it.






Tip1. What must a President do before using IEEPA’s powers?





Declare a national emergency under the National Emergencies Act over an unusual and extraordinary threat that originates largely outside the United States. See IEEPA.









Tip2. Why did Congress pass IEEPA in 1977?





Between 1933 and 1977 Section 5(b) of the Trading with the Enemy Act was used in peacetime emergencies as an all-purpose sanctions power. IEEPA moved peacetime use into a separate statute tied to the new emergency procedures.









Tip3. How did CAATSA change the President’s control of Russia sanctions?





Its Russia title wrote existing executive order sanctions into statute and gave Congress a procedure to block the President from easing them. See CAATSA.









Tip4. What does the Global Magnitsky Act let the executive do, and to whom?





Impose visa bans and asset freezes on foreign individuals and entities responsible for serious human rights abuse or significant corruption anywhere in the world. See Global Magnitsky Act.

The intelligence oversight system grew out of the 1970s investigations. It moved from Hughes-Ryan’s requirement of a presidential finding for CIA operations abroad to the current rule that the intelligence committees be kept fully and currently informed. After September 11, Congress separated leadership of the intelligence community from leadership of the CIA. Read this unit with the Title 10 and Title 50 page.

title: Unit 6: Intelligence and its oversight
text:
Further reading

Section 394 (cyber): Affirms the Defense Department’s authority to conduct military operations in cyberspace, including clandestine ones and ones short of hostilities, and classifies clandestine military cyber activity as traditional military activity instead of covert action.
Section 127e: Lets the Secretary of Defense fund foreign forces, irregular forces, groups, or individuals who support or facilitate ongoing U.S. special operations against terrorism.
FARA: A disclosure law. People who act in the United States on behalf of foreign governments, parties, or other foreign principals in political or public relations work must register with the Justice Department and report their activities and payments.

title: Unit 6: Intelligence and its oversight
text:
Key terms

Covert action

Activity to influence conditions abroad where the U.S. role is intended not to be apparent or acknowledged. It requires a written presidential finding and notice to the intelligence committees. Defined at 50 U.S.C. 3093(e).

Finding

A written presidential determination that a covert action is necessary to support identifiable foreign policy objectives.

Traditional military activities

The exception that keeps military operations out of the covert action definition, and with it outside the finding process.

title: Unit 6: Intelligence and its oversight
text:
Issues for Congress
Questions that recur in oversight and legislation, with the main arguments on each side. There is no answer key; they are for discussion and briefing preparation.

1. Should more members be told about the most sensitive covert actions?
The Intel Oversight Act lets the President limit notice of especially sensitive covert actions to eight congressional leaders.

Advocates of broader notice argue limited notification weakens oversight, because the leaders often cannot consult committee members or staff.
Defenders argue limited notice protects the most sensitive operations and sources, and that the full committees are informed in time.



2. How should Congress oversee military operations that resemble intelligence activities?
Clandestine military activity under authorities such as Section 127e and Section 394 (cyber) reports to the armed services committees, not through the covert action process.

Some argue the two oversight systems should share information or that notice rules should depend on the activity, not the agency conducting it.
Others argue the distinction reflects real differences in chain of command and acknowledgment, and that Congress has already added targeted notice rules on the Title 10 side.

title: Unit 6: Intelligence and its oversight
text:
Check yourself
Try to answer each question before opening it.






Tip1. What did the Hughes-Ryan Amendment require?





That no funds be spent on CIA operations abroad other than intelligence collection unless the President found the operation important to national security and reported it to Congress. It has been superseded. See Hughes-Ryan Amendment and Intel Oversight Act.









Tip2. What standard of notice does the oversight title of the National Security Act set?





The executive must keep the two intelligence committees fully and currently informed of intelligence activities, including significant anticipated ones. See Intel Oversight Act.









Tip3. What office did IRTPA create, and why?





The Director of National Intelligence, to separate leadership of the whole intelligence community from leadership of the CIA, as the 9/11 Commission recommended. See IRTPA.









Tip4. What problem does CIPA solve?





It sets pretrial and trial procedures for classified information in criminal cases, so a defendant cannot force the government to choose between dropping a case and disclosing secrets. See CIPA.

title: Unit 2: Building the national security state, 1947 to 1958
text:
Previous: Unit 1. Where the power comes from | All units | Next: Unit 3. Deciding to use force
In a little over a decade Congress created the National Security Council, the CIA, the Air Force, and a single Department of Defense, then gave that department a working chain of command. It also wrote one code of military justice, a standing draft law, and a tool for mobilizing industry. These are framework statutes: most later laws plug into the institutions they created.

National Security Act 1947 In force Framework statute
The founding charter of the modern national security system. It created the National Security Council and the Central Intelligence Agency, established a separate Air Force, and placed the military departments under a single Secretary of Defense.
Read it: enacted text, current code  I have read this


NSA Amendments (1949) 1949 In force Framework statute
Fixed the weak structure created in 1947. It turned the National Military Establishment into the Department of Defense, an executive department, and reduced the Army, Navy, and Air Force to military departments under the Secretary of Defense.
Read it: enacted text, current code  I have read this


CIA Act 1949 In force Framework statute
Gave the CIA the administrative tools to operate in secret: authority to spend money without the usual accounting rules, to withhold information about its staff and structure, and to procure and transfer funds confidentially.
Read it: enacted text, current code  I have read this


DoD Reorganization Act (1958) 1958 In force Framework statute
President Eisenhower’s reorganization. It took the military departments out of the operational chain of command, so that orders run from the President and the Secretary of Defense to unified commands, and it confirmed the Secretary’s authority, direction, and control over the whole department.
Read it: enacted text, current code  I have read this


UCMJ 1950 In force Framework statute
The criminal code and court system of the U.S. armed forces. It replaced the separate Army and Navy disciplinary codes with one law for all services, defining military offenses, the types of courts-martial, the rights of the accused, and civilian appellate review.
Read it: enacted text, current code  I have read this


Defense Production Act 1950 Partly expired Framework statute
A Korean War statute that lets the President direct private industry in the interest of national defense: by putting government orders first in line, by financing new production capacity, and by organizing industry cooperation.
Read it: enacted text, current code  I have read this


Selective Service Act 1948 Partly expired Framework statute
The standing law of conscription. It requires men to register at 18 and maintains the Selective Service System so that a draft could be run if Congress and the President restored the power to induct.

text:
Further reading

Smith-Mundt Act: The legal foundation of U.S. public diplomacy. It authorized the State Department to explain the United States to foreign audiences through broadcasting, publications, and educational and cultural exchanges.
Lend-Lease Act: Authorized the President to sell, transfer, lend, or lease defense articles to any country whose defense he judged vital to the defense of the United States.
Mutual Security Act: Merged the Marshall Plan’s economic aid, military assistance to allies, and technical assistance into one program under one agency, with the stated purpose of strengthening the free world against Soviet power.
Atomic Energy Act: The governing law for both civilian and military uses of nuclear material in the United States.

title: Unit 2: Building the national security state, 1947 to 1958
text:
Key terms

Framework statute

A standing law that creates an institution or a general procedure that later laws and executive actions depend on.

Operational chain of command

The line of authority for military operations, which since 1958 runs from the President through the Secretary of Defense to the unified commands, not through the service departments.

Unified combatant command

A command with forces from more than one service under a single commander, organized by region or function.

title: Unit 2: Building the national security state, 1947 to 1958
text:
Issues for Congress
Questions that recur in oversight and legislation, with the main arguments on each side. There is no answer key; they are for discussion and briefing preparation.

1. Does the 1947 structure still fit current threats, or is another reorganization due?
The structure created by the National Security Act has been revised by statute in 1949, 1958, 1986, and 2004.

Advocates of reorganization point to cyber, economic security, and technology competition, which cut across departments built for the Cold War.
Skeptics argue reorganizations are disruptive and slow to pay off, and that the framework adapts well through targeted amendments such as the Goldwater-Nichols Act and the IRTPA.



2. Should the Defense Production Act’s industrial authorities be made permanent?
Much of the Defense Production Act depends on periodic reauthorization.

Supporters of permanence argue that industrial base and supply chain needs are continuous and that lapses create uncertainty for industry.
Supporters of sunsets argue that reauthorization is Congress’s main opportunity to review how broad economic powers have been used.

title: Unit 2: Building the national security state, 1947 to 1958
text:
Check yourself
Try to answer each question before opening it.






Tip1. Name three things the National Security Act of 1947 created.





The National Security Council, the Central Intelligence Agency, and a separate Air Force, with the military departments placed under a single Secretary of Defense. See National Security Act.









Tip2. What did the 1949 amendments change?





They turned the loose National Military Establishment into the Department of Defense, an executive department, and reduced the Army, Navy, and Air Force to military departments under the Secretary. See NSA Amendments (1949).









Tip3. What did the 1958 reorganization do to the operational chain of command?





It took the military departments out of it, so that orders run from the President and Secretary of Defense to the unified commands. See DoD Reorganization Act (1958), and later Goldwater-Nichols Act.









Tip4. Which Korean War statute lets the government put defense orders first in line at private companies?





The Defense Production Act, which also finances new production capacity and organizes industry cooperation. Parts of it depend on periodic reauthorization.

FISA created a court process for foreign intelligence surveillance inside the United States. After September 11 Congress widened collection, then in 2008 added Section 702 for targeting foreigners abroad through U.S. providers, then in 2015 ended bulk telephone records collection. The live questions concern sunsets and how agencies may search lawfully collected data for Americans’ information.

Cyber Info Sharing Act: Enacted as Division N of the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2016. It set up a voluntary system for companies and the federal government to share cyber threat indicators and defensive measures, with legal protection for companies that take part.

title: Unit 7: Surveillance law
text:
Key terms

Section 702

The FISA authority, added in 2008, to target non-U.S. persons reasonably believed to be abroad with compelled help from U.S. providers, under annual court-approved certifications instead of individual orders.

U.S. person query

A search of lawfully collected data using a term associated with an American. RISAA’s changes concentrated on how the FBI may run them.

Sunset

A date on which an authority expires unless Congress extends it.

title: Unit 7: Surveillance law
text:
Issues for Congress
Questions that recur in oversight and legislation, with the main arguments on each side. There is no answer key; they are for discussion and briefing preparation.

1. Should searches of Section 702 data for Americans’ communications require a warrant?
A House amendment to require warrants failed on a tie vote during the 2024 reauthorization (RISAA), and the authority lapsed in June 2026.

Supporters of a warrant requirement argue that searching collected data for Americans’ communications is a search that should require a judge’s approval.
Opponents argue a warrant requirement would slow time-sensitive investigations, including of threats to Americans, and that court-approved procedures and oversight already protect privacy.



2. Given Clapper, how should surveillance programs be tested?
Clapper v. Amnesty made challenges to Section 702 in ordinary courts very difficult.

Some propose a larger role for the court-appointed amici created by the USA FREEDOM Act, or statutory standing for people likely to be affected.
Others argue the Foreign Intelligence Surveillance Court, the intelligence committees, and inspectors general provide adequate review without exposing sources and methods in litigation.

title: Title 10 and Title 50
text:
Each title has its own page: Title 10, Title 50, Title 22, and Title 32.
“Title 10” and “Title 50” are shorthand. Title 10 of the U.S. Code is Armed Forces: how the military is organized, commanded, trained, and used. Title 50 is War and National Defense: it holds the National Security Act, the CIA’s authorities, covert action and intelligence oversight, FISA, and also the War Powers Resolution and the emergency powers statutes.
In practice people use the labels to mean something narrower:









“Title 10”
“Title 50”




Kind of activity
Military operations
Intelligence activities, especially covert action


Typical actor
Armed forces under a military commander
CIA, or others acting under its authority


Chain of authority
President, Secretary of Defense, combatant commander
President, Director of the CIA, with the Director of National Intelligence overseeing the community


Approval
Orders through the military chain of command
Written presidential finding for covert action


Oversight committees
Armed Services
Intelligence


Deniability
U.S. role acknowledged, or at least able to be
U.S. role intended not to be acknowledged



The shorthand is imprecise in two ways. The Defense Department holds many Title 50 authorities, since the National Security Agency, the Defense Intelligence Agency, and the other defense intelligence agencies are part of it. And the same people and equipment can operate under either authority depending on who is directing the mission.

title: Title 10 and Title 50
section: The legal hinge: the definition of covert action
text:
The legal hinge: the definition of covert action
The line is drawn by one definition, added to the National Security Act in 1991 and now at 50 U.S.C. 3093(e). Covert action is activity to influence political, economic, or military conditions abroad where the U.S. role is intended not to be apparent or acknowledged. Covert action needs a written presidential finding and notice to the intelligence committees under the rules described on the Intelligence Oversight Act page.
The definition then excludes four categories. The one that matters here is “traditional diplomatic or military activities.” Anything that qualifies as a traditional military activity is not covert action, needs no finding, and is overseen by the armed services committees instead.
The statute does not define traditional military activities. The 1991 conference report described them as activities by military personnel under the direction and control of a U.S. military commander, before or during hostilities that are ongoing or anticipated, where the U.S. role in the overall operation is apparent or will be acknowledged. How far “anticipated” hostilities and “overall operation” stretch is the core of the dispute.
Two terms are often confused. A clandestine operation hides the operation itself. A covert operation hides who is behind it. Military special operations are routinely clandestine without being covert in the statutory sense.

title: Title 10 and Title 50
text:
Where the line is contested
Special operations outside war zones. Military preparation of the environment, such as reconnaissance and building local networks, can look identical to intelligence collection. Programs under Section 127e fund surrogate forces for counterterrorism and report to the armed services committees.
Cyber operations. Whether offensive cyber operations against an adversary’s networks in peacetime required a finding was argued for years. Section 394 answered it in 2018 by declaring clandestine military cyber activity a traditional military activity.
Mixed operations. The 2011 raid that killed Osama bin Laden was carried out by military personnel but, by official accounts, conducted under CIA authority. It is the standard illustration that the title describes the authority and chain of command for a mission, not the uniform worn by the people doing it.
Dual roles. One officer has served as both director of the National Security Agency and commander of U.S. Cyber Command, sitting in both systems at once.

title: Title 10 and Title 50
section: Why the distinction matters for oversight
text:
Why the distinction matters for oversight
The two committee systems see different things. Covert action comes with a statutory finding and prior notice. Military operations historically came with fewer formal notice rules, on the theory that they are acknowledged and run through an accountable chain of command.
Critics argue this creates an incentive to label sensitive activity as military in order to avoid the finding process. Defenders reply that military operations are subject to the law of armed conflict, the chain of command, and the Uniform Code of Military Justice, and that the intelligence framework was never meant to cover them.
Congress has responded by adding notice rules on the Title 10 side, one activity at a time: sensitive military operations (10 U.S.C. 130f), sensitive military cyber operations (10 U.S.C. 395), and special operations support programs. Most of these arrived through the annual defense authorization. The result is a patchwork that narrows the gap without merging the two systems.

title: Title 10 and Title 50
text:
Neighboring titles
The same kind of question, which title and therefore whose rules, comes up elsewhere in this wiki:

Title 10 and Title 22. Training and equipping foreign forces can be done by the Defense Department under Chapter 16 of Title 10 or by the State Department under the Foreign Assistance Act and Arms Export Control Act. The choice determines who decides, who pays, and which committees oversee it.
Title 10 and Title 32. National Guard members can serve under federal command or under their governor with federal funding. As the mobilization authorities page explains, the status decides whether the Posse Comitatus Act applies.
Title 50 and Title 18. Intelligence collection under FISA and criminal investigation run on different standards, and the wall between them has been raised and lowered several times.

title: Title 10 and Title 50
text:
Before you rely on this
The law never defines “traditional military activities,” and much of how the government draws the line in practice is classified. So even experts disagree on the details. This page lays out the debate without taking a side; check the linked statute pages and official sources before relying on a specific point.
